Katalog Berita (Halaman 7/57)

#10161. From the Hugging Face Hub to robot hardware with Strands Agents and LeRobot

A walkthrough of the LeRobot integration in Strands Robots - one agent loop, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot, with sim-to-real datasets in the same on-disk format and policies you swap with a string.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6, which rewrote the library around three classes: Simulation, Robot and Policy.

You have a robot, a folder of demonstration data on the Hugging Face Hub, and a new task you want it to learn. Today that takes five separate tools: one to record new demonstrations, another to train, a third to test in simulation, custom code to deploy on hardware, and yet another to coordinate when you have more than one robot. The pieces work on their own. They don't talk to each other.

Strands Robots is an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that gives you a robot, its simulation, and the LeRobot stack behind agent tools that you hand to a single Strands agent. The integration is deliberately thin: LeRobot's own scripts handle hardware recording and calibration, and Strands Robots comes in for the parts an agent actually orchestrates. A robot in simulation records LeRobotDatasets with LeRobot's own writer, in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. A Policy loads LeRobot checkpoints in-process behind one interface, including ACT, SmolVLA, pi0, GR00T and MolmoAct2. A peer mesh fans the agent out to remote robots. The dataset format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it; the agent loop is the glue.

This post walks you through five steps inside a single agent: build the agent over the robot's tools, record a demonstration as a LeRobotDataset in simulation, run a policy from the Hub on the same robot, deploy the same agent code to a physical SO-101 with one keyword argument change, and reach the robot over the Zenoh mesh. At the end, you can clone the working sample from GitHub and run it on your laptop in simulation. No hardware, no GPU, no Hugging Face credentials needed for the default path. The runnable companion to this post is the notebook notebooks/11_hub_to_hardware.ipynb.

Strands Robots gives you the LeRobot stack behind agent tools that you hand to one Strands agent. The example agent in this post does four things: drive a simulated SO-101 while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hub as a LeRobotDataset, run a policy from the Hub on that robot, and deploy the same agent code to a physical robot with one keyword argument change. When you have more than one robot, the agent can coordinate the whole fleet through a built-in peer mesh. For hardware recording and calibration, LeRobot's own CLIs (lerobot-record, lerobot-calibrate) handle the bring-up; the agent picks up from there.

Figure 1. Robot("so101") is an SO-101 in a MuJoCo world by default; Robot("so101", port=...) drives the physical arm through the same safety chain. The agent holds the robot's tools, run(record=...) writes a LeRobot v3 dataset with LeRobot's own writer, and a Policy loads a checkpoint from the Hub by name, so a dataset captured in sim and a dataset captured on hardware use the same on-disk format.

Two design choices make this work. First, Robot("so101") is a robot in a simulated world by default (no hardware, no risk), and Robot("so101", port=...) is the same class driving a physical arm. The agent code is identical across both, and every command from the agent passes the robot's safety chain: a target outside a joint's range is refused, never clipped. Second, recording goes through LeRobot's own dataset writer on both the simulation path and hardware, so a dataset captured in MuJoCo and one captured from a physical SO-101 are in the same format.

The whole workflow in five lines of Python:

What follows is what's actually happening inside that call, step by step.

That's it. The example in this post runs end-to-end on a laptop with these three.

Install Strands Robots and get the example files:

Sign in to Hugging Face if you want to push datasets to the Hub. This is optional for the default simulation path in this post; the example runs end-to-end with a placeholder motion and writes the dataset to a local folder without needing Hub access.

The runnable example lives at notebooks/11_hub_to_hardware.ipynb, with the same code as a script in notebooks/scripts/11_hub_to_hardware.py, in the strands-labs/robots repository alongside the other numbered notebooks. The notebook is the recommended starting point: open it in JupyterLab and run cells top-to-bottom in simulation without any hardware connected.

A robot in simulation records LeRobotDatasets in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. No hardware required. robot.run(policy, record=...) writes a LeRobot v3 dataset through LeRobot's own writer, one episode per run: same parquet schema for joint states and actions, same per-camera MP4 layout. Recording is an argument your code passes, not something the agent decides, so the operator chooses what is kept:

Pass a folder (record="data/cube_picking_sim") instead to keep the dataset local.

Figure 2. The recording scene in MuJoCo simulation: the SO-101 arm and a red cube on the ground plane, captured to a LeRobotDataset. No hardware, no GPU, no Hugging Face credentials needed for this default path.

The placeholder motion is intentional: it moves the arm so the workflow runs end-to-end without a trained checkpoint. The robot waves rather than completing the grasp, and the recording is structurally complete (valid joint states, valid camera frames, a well-formed LeRobotDataset episode), but the demonstration itself isn't useful as training data. Step 3 below swaps in a trained policy from the Hub; the recording call, dataset format, and agent code stay the same.

The proof is what happens next. LeRobot's own dataset loader reads the sim-recorded data with no Strands-specific code path:

These features are the same as any LeRobot dataset on the Hub: same column names, same parquet+MP4 layout, same loader path, plus time.measured, the time each frame was actually read, so a stall shows up in the data. Training scripts that consume hardware-recorded data consume the sim-recorded data without modification. Datasets pushed from sim sit alongside hardware recordings in the same Hub repository if you want them to.

A single episode from a recorded LeRobotDataset, played back from the per-camera MP4 LeRobot's writer produced, the same on-disk video a training script reads.

To record demonstrations on a physical SO-101 instead of simulation, use LeRobot's record CLI directly. Strands Robots doesn't wrap that command because LeRobot already does the job cleanly:

The dataset that lands on the Hub from this command is in the same format as the simulation recording. To fine-tune a policy on it, run LeRobot's training CLI (lerobot-train); training itself is out of scope for this post and follows the standard LeRobot workflow. From Step 3 onward, the agent picks up either the original or a fine-tuned checkpoint interchangeably. For full SO-101 hardware setup, calibration, and cameras, see the hardware guide.

With the dataset on the Hub, the next step is to run a policy. A Hub repo id is a policy: Policy("/") loads a LeRobot checkpoint in-process with LeRobot's own loader. You hand it to the robot's tool by name, and the agent runs it the same way it would run any other policy:

Under the hood, the agent calls the robot tool's run action with policy="act". The robot steps the simulation with the policy's action chunks, and every action passes the same safety chain as a command from the agent. norm= states the units the checkpoint was trained in, and the library checks it against the checkpoint's saved statistics before the first step, naming the joint and the fix if they disagree. The chain applies to the policy too: in one of our runs it stopped the checkpoint after 1.3 seconds, when it asked for the gripper 0.0002 rad past its range, and the robot refused the step instead of clipping it. To run inference on a separate GPU machine instead, serve the checkpoint with LeRobot's lerobot-policy-server and point the robot at it with Policy("zenoh://gpu-box:7447/").

Figure 3. The Hub ACT checkpoint driving the simulated SO-101. It was trained on a real SO-101 with a wrist camera, so here it moves the arm; a checkpoint trained on your own demonstrations swaps in by changing the string.

A different checkpoint is a different string. Policy runs ACT, Diffusion, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T and MolmoAct2 checkpoints, anything LeRobot's own policy registry can load. The policy guide lists the families and the options.

Note: Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust.

This is the same code as Step 3, with one keyword argument changed. port= gives the same Robot class a Feetech driver for the physical arm, with LeRobot's calibration file:

The same agent prompt now runs against a physical arm. The camera names are the image keys the policy sees, and on a real arm nothing moves without the operator: operator= is asked once for every move a tool requests, and once for a policy run's plan. The same checkpoint, loaded in-process, generates the action chunks.

Before this runs against your SO-101, calibration for both follower and leader has to be in place. Run LeRobot's calibration command (lerobot-calibrate) once per device; the files land under ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/ and Robot(..., id=...) reads them from there. If a calibration is missing, the robot says which file it looked for.

Up to now we've driven one robot at a time. The mesh is how Strands Robots handles more than one. Picture five SO-101s running the same warehouse task in parallel, a humanoid coordinating with a mobile base, or an arm in another room that an agent on your laptop drives. All of those are mesh patterns. The mesh is built on Zenoh, an open source peer-to-peer protocol, and you don't manage IP addresses, write discovery code, or pick a broker; robots show up on the mesh the moment they're mounted, and the agent can talk to all of them at once.

A robot joins a mesh when you mount it, and the agent reaches every robot on the mesh through one tool, use_mesh:

The agent lists the devices on the mesh, reads each one's manifest, and invokes the same actions the robot's own tool has: observe, act, run, stop and estop. Use Mesh("iot://us-west-2") with the iot extra to route the same calls over AWS IoT Core for cross-network fleets; the agent code doesn't change.

Safety goes with the robot, not the transport. An agent can always press e-stop, on one robot or with a broadcast to all of them, but it can never resume one: only a named operator can, with resume(approved_by=...). A plain zenoh:// mesh is one any machine on the network can join, so a real robot on it is observe-only until you give the lab certificates (python -m strands_robots.mesh ca and cert); simulated robots take commands on it freely.

The transport scales without touching agent code. On the LAN, Zenoh peers find each other with no broker. Across subnets, run a zenohd router with its own certificate, and for cloud fleets the iot:// mesh carries the same calls over AWS IoT Core with an X.509 certificate per robot.

The full sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in the notebooks/ folder. Notebook 11 packages all five steps, with the same code as a script in notebooks/scripts/11_hub_to_hardware.py. It runs in simulation with a placeholder motion and a small ACT checkpoint from the Hub. No GPU, no Docker, no Hugging Face credentials needed.

The agent steps use Amazon Bedrock with your AWS credentials; set STRANDS_MODEL_ID to the model you want. The recorded dataset lands in a temporary folder the notebook prints. To push it to the Hugging Face Hub instead of keeping it local, set HF_USER= after hf auth login with write scope.

The code snippets shown in this setup represent a “hello world” example of setting up Strands Robots with HuggingFace. For more serious, production-ready use cases there are some important considerations users should be aware of:

Supplying untrusted data into agents can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. Given the actuation of these robots in physical space, this is an important risk to track. To mitigate this behavior, developers should be careful to feed the robots only data that comes from a trusted source. If not all input data can be trusted, developers should restrict the tools available to the agent to prevent the robots from making safety-critical actions.

A plain zenoh:// mesh, as in the snippets in this post, has no access control: any device on the same network can join it, and the peer id in a request is only a claim. That is why a real robot on it answers only describe, observe, stop and estop. For untrusted networks or production environments, give each machine a lab certificate (python -m strands_robots.mesh ca, then cert), so the mesh runs over mutual TLS and only machines with a certificate can reach a robot. On AWS IoT Core, give each robot its own X.509 certificate and an IoT policy limited to its own topics.

On a real robot, operator= is the gate: one function answers every move a tool, the dashboard or the mesh asks for, and every policy run's plan, once, before anything moves. The agent's approval never comes from its own tool arguments, so a prompt-injection attempt that slips an approval into a command cannot bypass it. An agent can always press e-stop but can never release one, calibrate, record, push, or choose a policy address on the network, and it loads a Hub checkpoint by name only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS.

The preceding workflow opens serial ports on hardware and writes a local dataset cache. To return your environment to a clean state:

The integration's central design choice is that Strands Robots doesn't reimplement what LeRobot already provides. Calibration, the dataset format, and the policies stay upstream. Strands adds the agent tools, the safety chain and the mesh that make them composable from natural language.

Two consequences follow. For users, every dataset on the Hub is an asset an agent can extend, fine-tune from, and deploy against with no conversion step. For developers, simulation data and hardware data share a single file format, so training scripts written for one consume the other unchanged. The line between sim and real becomes a deployment detail, not an architectural divide.

Figure 4. The Strands Robots catalog spans arms, humanoids, mobile bases, and hands, all in the same MuJoCo simulation and behind the same Robot class. The SO-101 in this post is one of its 76 robot presets.

The full Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. For larger workloads, Strands Robots also runs GPU simulation: MuJoCo-Warp with Simulation("mujoco", physics="newton") and Isaac Sim with Simulation("isaac"). Both sit behind the same Robot class shown in this post, so the agent code stays the same as you scale up.

Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this workflow, open an issue with what worked and what didn't. The SDK improves fastest when developer feedback lands directly on the surface that needs it.

Cagatay Cali is a Research Engineer at AWS focused on Agentic AI and robotics. He designs interfaces that connect AI agents to physical robots, enabling developers to control robotic systems through natural language and making agents and robotics development accessible to builders at any skill level.

Sundar Raghavan is a Sr Solutions Architect at AWS on the Agentic AI Foundations team. He leads the developer experience for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, owning the SDK and CLI, and drives the framework and ecosystem integrations strategy. He focuses on how developers build, deploy, and scale production AI agents on AWS. He is currently extending that focus into physical AI, collaborating on Strands Robots to bring the same agent developer experience to robotics.

Fantastic to see! The single-kwarg flip from MuJoCo sim to mode="real" (same agent code, same LeRobotDataset format end to end) is exactly the friction-removal that gets robotics agents into real labs. Work like this lifts all the ships: the easier and more open we make agent-to-hardware control, the faster the whole industry moves. The Device Connect team at Arm is excited to collaborate!

#10160. A Preflight Checklist for Shipping 3D Models on the Web

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A 3D model that looks smooth in a desktop modeling application can become a very different experience inside a web page. The browser must download the asset, decode its geometry and textures, upload resources to the GPU, compile materials and render the scene while the rest of the page stays responsive.

Consider an ecommerce team adding a rotatable chair model to a product page. The asset works well on a developer's laptop, but the first mobile test shows a long blank interval, a sharp increase in memory use and uneven rotation. The problem is not necessarily the JavaScript viewer. The model itself may contain more data than the page can comfortably deliver.

A preflight process catches these issues before the asset is connected to production code. This checklist walks through it, and includes a small, tested script that audits a GLB file against a budget. Tool details change, so check each project's documentation for current behavior.

For the chair, rotation may help shoppers inspect the rear frame, arm shape and the relationship between the seat and legs. That is a clear use. Adding the same model as a moving background behind the product description would add download and rendering costs without equivalent value.

Define the purpose before setting a performance budget. A featured product viewer may justify more detail than a small decorative object. The decision also affects whether the model should load immediately, wait until the user scrolls near it or appear only after someone selects "View in 3D."

Editable authoring files often contain information a browser does not need, so web delivery should use an asset prepared for runtime rather than the original scene from a modeling application.

The Khronos glTF specification describes glTF as a format designed for efficient transmission and loading of 3D scenes and models. A .gltf asset can reference separate buffers and images, while a binary .glb file can package the scene and its resources into one file.

GLB is convenient when a team wants a single deployable asset, but a single container does not guarantee a small payload. Large textures, dense geometry, unused animations and unnecessary scene objects can still make the file expensive. Document the format decision along with supported materials, texture limits, coordinate conventions and animation requirements.

Before debugging React components, shaders or loading logic, confirm that the file itself behaves as expected. Several free viewers can open a model in the browser for a quick visual check:

Whichever you use, rotate the chair, zoom in and inspect it from above, below and behind. This check can reveal obvious problems:

A viewer is useful for visual inspection, but it is not a performance profiler or automatic repair tool. A model can display correctly while still being too heavy for the intended page. Viewers also differ in lighting and material handling, so confirm the final look in your own renderer.

Open the model in an appropriate inspection or editing tool and review what it contains. A product model should not carry unused lights, cameras, hidden prototypes, duplicate meshes or animation clips left over from production. These elements can increase file size, complicate traversal or create confusing behavior after import.

Check the object hierarchy as well. Hundreds of separately transformed parts can increase CPU work and draw-call overhead even if the total polygon count looks reasonable. At the same time, combining every surface into one mesh can make material changes or interaction difficult. If users can change the chair's upholstery and frame independently, those areas need useful separation. Decorative components that never change may not.

Triangle count matters, but it is only one part of the cost. A model with moderate geometry and several large uncompressed textures may use more memory than a denser mesh with efficient textures. Transparent materials, multiple lights, shadows and many separate materials can also affect rendering performance.

Establish budgets by device class and use case rather than copying one universal limit. A hero asset viewed full-screen has different requirements from twelve models displayed in a product grid.

Several of those numbers can be read straight from the file. The Node.js script below reads a GLB's JSON chunk, counts triangles, meshes, primitives, materials, textures, images, animations and cameras, and compares them with a budget. It has no dependencies and runs on current Node.js versions.

The test builds a small GLB in memory, confirms the triangle count (a line primitive is ignored), and checks that a too-low triangle budget, a stray camera and an unwanted animation are all flagged:

Run the test with node test_glb_budget.mjs, and audit a real file with node glb_budget.mjs chair.glb.

Textures often account for much of a 3D asset's download and memory footprint. Inspect every map and ask whether its resolution matches the size at which the surface will actually appear. A 4K texture may be wasteful if the chair occupies only a few hundred pixels on a phone. Multiple surfaces may be able to share a smaller atlas, and detail that is never visible can be removed.

Do not lower every texture to the same resolution automatically. The seat fabric may need more detail than the underside of the frame. Test reductions on the real page at normal viewing distances.

Material count also deserves attention. A separate material can produce another rendering operation even when it differs only slightly from another surface. Consolidate materials where doing so does not remove required customization.

A product page should not delay its primary text, price, photographs and purchase controls while downloading a below-the-fold 3D asset. Use an explicit interaction or an IntersectionObserver to begin loading when the viewer approaches the viewport. A simplified pattern looks like this:

The positive margin starts the request shortly before the viewer becomes visible. The appropriate value depends on page layout, model size and expected network speed. Display a meaningful poster image while loading, so the page stays useful if the asset fails, WebGL is unavailable or the user prefers not to spend bandwidth on the interactive view.

Using the device's full pixel ratio can make a canvas unnecessarily expensive on high-density screens. Cap the rendering resolution and evaluate the visual difference on actual devices. Shadows, environment maps, antialiasing and post-processing should also be treated as adjustable costs. A desktop may use the complete presentation, while a lower-powered phone receives simpler lighting and reduced texture resolution.

Avoid guessing from a user-agent string. Where possible, choose conservative defaults, observe runtime performance and let the experience degrade gracefully. Pause rendering when the viewer is outside the viewport or the browser tab is hidden, since a product model does not need to consume GPU time while the customer reads specifications farther down the page.

A model that performs well in isolation may struggle when combined with analytics scripts, image carousels, embedded video and the rest of the production page. Test on real phones, not only through desktop emulation, and include a mid-range device and a throttled network. Measure the time until the poster appears, the time until the model becomes interactive, frame consistency during rotation, and whether the page stays responsive during decoding.

Use browser performance and network tools to separate bottlenecks. A slow download suggests a payload problem. A long main-thread task may point to parsing or scene initialization. Low frame rates after loading may indicate excessive draw calls, shader cost, overdraw or high rendering resolution. Repeat the test after each significant optimization, because a smaller file is useful only if the model still communicates the product accurately.

Interactive content should enhance the product page rather than become its only usable representation. Provide well-composed images, descriptive product text and accessible controls alongside the viewer. Keyboard users should be able to reach and operate relevant controls, while motion should not begin unexpectedly or continue without purpose. If the 3D experience fails, the customer should still be able to understand the chair and complete the intended task.

GLB packages everything in one file, which is convenient to deploy. Separate .gltf files let you cache buffers and images independently. Neither guarantees a small payload.

No. A viewer confirms how a model looks, not how it performs. Measure size, textures, draw calls and load time in the real page.

There is no universal number. Set budgets by device class and by how prominent the model is on the page, then test on a mid-range phone.

Shipping 3D on the web is ultimately a delivery problem. The model, textures, loading strategy, renderer, device and surrounding page all contribute to the result. A disciplined preflight process prevents teams from treating a successful desktop preview as proof of production readiness, and gives users the benefits of interactive 3D without making the rest of the page pay an unreasonable price.

#10159. Is it agentic enough? Benchmarking open models on your own tooling

Benchmarking transformers revisions across different metrics

This is a human-made, agent-focused blogpost.

Coding agents increasingly work with our software instead of us: describe a task, and the agent picks the library, writes the calls, runs them, and debugs its own mistakes. When the library gets in the way, it will happily bypass it and rewrite the logic from scratch. This introduces a new concept in library development: the code should not only be correct and fast, but should be designed so that an agent can drive it effectively. A clunky API or stale docs annoy us developers, but it now also sends the agent down a longer, more expensive path.

Most benchmarks just look at the final answer. We wanted the whole process instead: not just whether the agent got it right, but how much work it took to get there, and how that shifts across models, library revisions, and tasks. We measured exactly that, using transformers as our case study.

Here, we will introduce a tool specific benchmark focusing on how the answer was found, and provide a simple implementation of one such harness, running entirely on open models driven by the pi coding agent, with the full sweep of models × revisions × tasks fanned out across Hugging Face Jobs so every run sees identical hardware.

But, how do you optimize software for agents?

We're strong believers in the following two software principles:

This remains the same within the realm of agentic-optimized tooling, and, for once, the two are directly tied to each other.

You want your tool to exist for an agent: it needs to be discoverable. The API needs to be clear and the docs need to be extensive. They need to be structured in a way that the agent has rapid access to the useful files and examples. If you want your tool to work for an agent, then you should test it for agentic-use.

We'll use transformers as an example throughout this blogpost: agents using it to solve ML tasks (classifying text, captioning images, transcribing audio), not contributing code to it; though the harness was designed to work with any tool that can be operated from the command line.

Our intuition on transformers was that usage could be dramatically simplified with a few changes: a CLI, a Skill, and self-contained, task-specific examples. This is the same recipe recently applied to the hf CLI, redesigned to be agent-optimized, where agents used 1.3–1.8× (and up to 6×) fewer tokens. We wanted to know whether that kind of win generalizes, and whether it could be useful for transformers as well.

Intuition is a powerful tool, but we wanted more evidence before we opened PRs that add several thousand lines of code to such a widely used codebase as transformers. We set out to measure what success looks like.

Two agents can both produce the correct label for a sentiment-classification task, but one:

Both reach POSITIVE (0.9999), and here are the two paths an agent actually took on this exact task:

Both methods reach the same result. But they have very different profiles in cost, latency, token usage, and failures.

If your evaluation only checks the final string, you're blind to these as well as whether a change you shipped to the library (a CLI improvement, better error messages, a Skill) actually helped agents.

Our goal with this harness is to evaluate how much work an agent has to do to perform a given task, and whether changes to the library improve performance.

A few words on how we'll evaluate agents here.

We run every task under three variants (or "tiers"); three different ways an agent can come at transformers:

These aren't nested: skill doesn't contain clone (it ships curated docs, not the source tree), and neither strictly contains the other, each gives the agent a different kind of help. As we'll see, a model can sometimes do better on clone than on skill.

Not all models driving agents are equal, and their difference changes what you should look at when running them.

At one end, you have the largest, most capable open models. On reasonably common tasks, these should get the right answer, eventually. For them, task completion saturates near 100% and stops telling you much about your tool; a more relevant benchmark is the effort it took the agent to get there: how many turns, tokens and seconds it took, and whether they walked a clean path or used deprecated APIs.

Local models vary widely in size, and so do their abilities. Metrics such as "match %" are more relevant than for their larger counterparts, as you can see how model sizes/capabilities affect results on your specific tool.

This harness not only provides guidance to library maintainers on how to improve a repository for agent interactions, it also helps assess how different agents and models perform on the tasks users care about.

The harness scores every run on several axes, so that you can ask what actually matters for each class of model:

All of it lands in a report you can directly examine:

The live report: Overview, Coverage, and Results, all client-side.

And because it captures the native agent trace of every run, numbers are just the beginning: you can read exactly what the agent did, command by command. The traces are shareable through the Hub's agent-traces viewer:

A run rendered in the Hub's agent-traces viewer: MiniMax-M2.7 on the answer-question task. Open this trace on the Hub ↗

Before the results, a quick recap of the setup. Each run varies four things: the model driving the agent, the transformers revision it runs against, the task, and the tier (bare / clone / skill). As discussed, we look at different metrics for the two different model categories.

Since a large open model will usually get to the correct result, what you're really measuring is the effort it took to do so. Did it take ten turns or one? Did it follow an API path you deprecated because it trusted obsolete documentation? Did it hit an error you hadn't foreseen?

The natural experiment is to fix one strong model and vary the tool's revisions: the successive git versions of transformers we test against, from released tags like v5.8.0 and v5.9.0 to the specific commit that introduces the CLI and Skill. We want to watch whether the load it puts on the agent goes up or down. We used the harness on transformers to check whether adding a dedicated CLI and Skill actually lightened the agents' work.

For the three large models we used in our tests, the average time spent on all tasks indicates that the Skill commit results in less time spent working on the tasks:

Median time per revision, by tier: the skill commit (green dot) is the fastest.

On the other hand, in the experiments in which we cloned the repository, we can see a significant increase in token consumption due to the commit that introduced the CLI and examples, as we'll see in a moment.

Median new tokens per revision, by tier: the clone variant jumps once the CLI lands in the repo.

Reading the clone-variant traces explains why. The commit adds a command, but it also ships the CLI's implementation and a set of cli/agentic/*.py usage examples into the repository directly.

On the clone variant the agent has a full transformers checkout in front of it, and roughly a third of the runs go read the new surface (the /cli/ tree and the example scripts) to learn the interface before calling it. This raises the median input from ~4k to ~6.4k tokens.

The two charts are then two sides of one tradeoff: the commit buys the large models less time (they reach for the CLI instead of debugging Python) at the cost of more tokens (they read the code that taught them the CLI). A tradeoff worth knowing about before merging PRs.

One caveat works in the CLI's favor, though, which isn't benchmarked yet: the cost of reading it is amortized with successive runs. Our setup is built for one-off experiments. Each run is a fresh agent that rediscovers the CLI from scratch, so it pays the discovery cost every time. In real usage an agent learns the interface once and then solves task after task within the same session, amortizing that cost across many requests. The token bump we measure here is closer to a worst case than to what a user would see day to day.

Open models give us fine-grained control over the variables that matter most here: size, configuration, quantization, provider, training, and anything that would differ from one model to the next. They're also where a good tool surface matters most: a small model asked to "use transformers to do X" on a bare environment can guess an API that changed some releases ago, may do unnecessary tool calls, and can get the wrong answer.

So here the experiment is the opposite of the above: hold the revision and sweep the model. This helps see which models actually take care of the task, not just by token count and time, but down to which ones can't reliably handle the tool calls. Our intuition is that the smaller the model, the harder both tool use and the task get; we ran the harness across a range of model sizes to test exactly that:

Match % across models, by tier: the skill tier lifts the larger models but drops the smaller ones.

which also seems to be correlated with the number of tokens ingested

Median new tokens across models, by tier.

A note on fair comparison: naively averaging across tasks is misleading when coverage is uneven (a model that only finished the quick tasks looks fast). The report has a "shared tasks only" toggle (across models and/or revisions) so you compare like-for-like, and a Coverage heatmap so you can see exactly which task × revision × model cells actually ran.

Two things come together here: how to look past whether the agent succeeded to what it did and how it did it; as well as the first results we pulled out of the harness.

Match %, tokens, and time tell you the cost of a run but don't tell you much about what happened under the hood.

This is why we've introduced the concept of markers. A marker is a named pattern the profile (the small per-tool plugin that teaches the harness how to build and drive a given library) matches against a run.

It is a one-line label for a behavior you care about, checked against the shell commands the agent ran, the code it wrote, the files it read, or its final answer. A run can fire several markers or none; the report shows how often each one fired, per model and per revision.

For transformers we declare a handful but we'll only look at the two most relevant ones:

These are what we watch to see whether a change actually shifted the agent's behavior. Interestingly here, the larger the model, the more it leverages the new context instead of using its memory; therefore leveraging the newly introduced CLI.

CLI adoption by tier across models: only the skill tier reaches for it, and more so as models grow.

CLI adoption is new: the CLI lands in a single commit, isn't in any model's training data, and is only lightly documented. The effect is clear: it's the Skill variant, the one that ships the CLI's documentation, that actually reaches for it, at 55.3%.

Comparing the commit across model sizes, the CLI + Skill helps the bigger models: on the skill tier, Kimi and the other large agents reach for the CLI and finish in fewer turns. (On clone they spend more input tokens first, reading the new CLI code, as we saw above, so the win shows up in time and turns, not raw tokens.)

Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.1, and MiniMax-M2.7 across revisions

But in some smaller-model settings, it appears to hurt performance. One plausible explanation is that small models lean on memorized API patterns, reproducing pipeline(...) snippets they've seen in their training data. The new concepts are then a larger surface for them to get wrong. You can watch this directly on the harness: lower match %, more retries, the cli marker barely firing. It is particularly striking on the Qwen3-4B model: the Skill barely changes its match rate yet its cost distribution is significantly affected.

Almost all of that comes from the clone tier. The checkout now contains the CLI's implementation and cli/agentic/*.py examples, and the 4B agent reads them in bulk: its median new tokens jump from ~2.4k to ~23k, with time and output skyrocketing as well, for no gain in accuracy.

Qwen3-4B across revisions. The CLI + Skill commit fans the cost distribution wide open, on the clone tier the agent reads the newly-shipped CLI source in bulk (~10× the new tokens), for no gain in match %. (repeat tokens stays flat: this setup uses no prompt caching.)

Sometimes, though, the Skill breaks correctness outright. Reading the traces shows how, for example for Qwen3-14B: adding the Skill drops its overall match rate from 67% (bare) to 43%, and on the simplest tasks the collapse is very visible: classify-sentiment goes from 100% on the clone variant to 0% with the Skill.

Qwen3-14B on classify-sentiment, by tier: clone (blue) holds at 100% across revisions, but the Skill variant (green) collapses to 0% at the CLI + Skill revision.

Looking at the traces, the model mistakes the CLI for a tool it can call directly (as in an agentic-harness tool, like web-search). The Skill is not an executable tool: it's documentation loaded into the agent's context, and the transformers CLI is only ever meant to be run from the shell (via bash); so this will not work.

Qwen3-14B reads the Skill and, in 39 of its 56 Skill runs, either emits a transformers(command="classify", ...) tool call (a tool that was never registered) or, finding nothing like it among its read/bash/edit/write tools, concludes it can't run a model and gives up. Either way, rather than fall back to the one-line pipeline(...) that scored 100% on the clone checkout, it declares the task impossible.

Qwen3-14B on classify-sentiment (Skill variant): it reasons that read/bash/edit/write can't run a model, and gives up.

This is exactly what we built the harness to catch: the same change that speeds the large models ends up breaking the small ones, which seemed a bit counterintuitive to us at first and something we'd likely have shipped as-is. The takeaway for maintainers: agent-facing APIs should be evaluated across model sizes, because a new affordance can reduce work for strong models while adding ambiguity for smaller ones. It also hints at a fix: rather than hand-write a Skill and check it after the fact, you could generate and validate one against the weaker models up front.

This is exactly what Upskill does: it turns a strong model's solution into a Skill only when it measurably helps the smaller ones.

The harness is one CLI, agent-eval. Install it, run a suite, fan it out across models × revisions on HF Jobs, and publish the report as a Hugging Face Space.

Trusted local use only. The harness runs a coding agent with bypassed permissions and executes code from whatever revision you point it at, and traces can contain prompts, output, and local paths. See SECURITY.md before pointing it at code you didn't write or sharing results.

The full, kept-current setup and usage instructions live in the README.

Checking the final answer tells you whether an agent can use your library. It doesn't tell you what it costs: the turns, tokens, errors, and the path it took to get there. This harness measures that, across the revisions and models you pick.

On transformers, it caught something we'd have shipped on faith: the CLI + Skill helps the largest open models and hurts the smallest ones. Worth knowing before merging!

It's profile-based, and designed to be adaptable: point it at your own library, define a few tasks and their expected answers, get the same report. Code and tasks are in the repo, traces are on the Hub. Let us know if you use it for your project!

This harness stands entirely on pi, Mario Zechner's coding-agent CLI: it drives every open-model run, and only needs an HF_TOKEN to serve a model, which is what made the open-model sweep practical at all.

Thanks to the model builders and inference providers behind the models we swept. Across the board they performed well above what the bare baseline would suggest.

#10156. Beyond LoRA: Can you beat the most popular fine-tuning technique?

If you want to fine-tune an open model on your own data, you are probably interested in so-called parameter-efficient fine-tuning, in short PEFT. This term describes techniques that significantly reduce the memory requirement to fine-tune a model. Although there are dozens of these techniques, almost everyone chooses one called “LoRA”. In this blog post, we explore whether LoRA is really the best choice, what tools are available to make an informed decision, and how you can benefit from extending your horizon beyond LoRA.

There are countless open models available, but they often aren't quite good enough for your use case. Prompting may help, but it usually isn't enough. Rather than training a new model from scratch, you should consider fine-tuning an existing one.

Fine-tuning, however, is memory-hungry: you generally need enough memory to fit the whole model several times over. Quantization reduces a model's memory footprint, but quantized models can't be fine-tuned directly. So a set of techniques emerged to cut the memory needed for fine-tuning, called "parameter-efficient fine-tuning", or PEFT.

With PEFT, you can fine-tune a model using only a fraction of that memory and even fine-tune quantized models. It offers other advantages, such as tiny checkpoint sizes, greater resistance to catastrophic forgetting, and the ability to serve multiple fine-tunes from the same base model.

At Hugging Face, we develop the PEFT library, which implements many PEFT techniques behind a unified API and integrates well with the ecosystem, for example Transformers and Diffusers. It also supports multiple quantization methods, enabling further accessibility in parameter-efficient fine-tuning. PEFT provides a good starting point, whether you want to fine-tune on your own data or you're researching a new PEFT method.

One parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that emerged early and proved to be quite effective is called “Low Rank Adaptation”, or short “LoRA”. It works by adding a handful of parameters on top of the base model, freezing the base model weights, and only training those few parameters.

Among all PEFT techniques, LoRA is by far the most popular. Here are a few estimates:

Although these estimates are not perfect, the conclusion is nonetheless that LoRA is almost certainly by far the most common PEFT technique.

This could just mean that LoRA works best for everyone, and this fact is reflected in its usage statistics. There is, however, another possibility: LoRA was one of the earlier, popular PEFT techniques. So maybe its usage became self-reinforcing: LoRA has the highest visibility, the highest number of tutorials/examples, and it has the best support in downstream packages. Thus LoRA's popularity feeds on itself.

This all leads to the question: Are we all leaving performance on the table by shunning better techniques? After all, there are countless researchers whose papers claim their technique beats LoRA. Isn't that sufficient proof that we should go beyond LoRA in favor of newer techniques?

There are dozens of papers that investigate fine-tuning techniques other than LoRA. Just in the PEFT library, there are more than 40 distinct PEFT techniques at the time of writing (and numerous more when counting variations of PEFT techniques). For almost all of them, you will find researchers claiming that their technique beats LoRA according to their benchmarks.

The trouble with these claims is that researchers are under pressure to provide results that beat the existing benchmark. Even without ill intent, this can bias the results, e.g. by spending less time tuning the alternative techniques compared to the one proposed by the researchers. One study found, for instance, that LoRA can match supposedly better PEFT techniques by tuning the learning rate.

Another complication is that each paper chooses a different set of PEFT techniques to compare to, and a different set of benchmarks to run. And even if the same technique is compared on the same benchmark, the code is often not available or not easy to run yourself, which makes results hard to reproduce.

Overall, it's difficult to figure out the PEFT technique that works best for you by only checking paper results. Therefore, you might be tempted to just go with the default, LoRA.

At Hugging Face, we thought about how we can help users make informed decisions about which PEFT technique to use. With the PEFT library, we already provide a package that implements many PEFT techniques and exposes them with the same API. The next step is to provide benchmarks that can shed more light on the discussed issue.

We already had a benchmark that checks fine-tuning of LLMs on a math dataset for some time. This benchmark takes an LLM and fine-tunes it on chain-of-thought reasoning to produce the result to a mathematical question using a base model that is not instruction fine-tuned. The benchmark thus checks if the model can learn to perform mathematical reasoning and also to adjust the generated output to the expected format.

To extend our findings on another modality, we also added an image generation benchmark. This one tests whether the model can be fine-tuned to learn a new concept, a cat plushy, and generate it in new contexts without forgetting existing concepts.

All PEFT techniques are evaluated according to the exact same conditions: same base model, same dataset, same training and evaluation code, same hardware. As different users have different needs, we track more than just test performance. Besides VRAM usage, we track metrics like forgetting/drift, runtime, and checkpoint size. The results are designed to run on consumer hardware, and adding a new experiment only requires adding a new PEFT config and running a script.

Since we compare all PEFT techniques on equal footing and have no horse in the race, we believe that these benchmarks can draw an objective picture of how well different PEFT techniques work. We argue that if you have your own dataset, you can take a similar approach and take advantage of the PEFT library to evaluate multiple PEFT techniques.

After finishing the benchmark runs, we found that although LoRA works well, other PEFT methods can beat it on one or multiple axes and should thus be considered. Check the image below that compares the performance of LoRA and five other PEFT techniques.

One way to interpret the results above is to think in terms of tradeoffs, for example: How well does the model perform on the test set vs how much memory is needed to train it? If a PEFT technique cannot be beaten on both of these metrics at the same time by any other technique, it is on the Pareto Frontier. In other words: If you want better test accuracy, you need more memory, and if you want more memory efficiency, you have to give up on accuracy.

Let's take a closer look at the results for the LLM Math dataset benchmark. When it comes to test accuracy vs memory, we find that LoRA is indeed on the Pareto frontier. It achieves 53.2% test accuracy and requires 22.6 GB of VRAM at the peak. There are, however, other PEFT techniques on the Pareto Frontier. For instance, BEFT achieves 32.9% test accuracy and requires only 20.2 GB of memory at max. On the other end, we have Lily, which achieves 54.9% test accuracy but requires 25.6 GB of memory. Depending on what's more important to you, you may conclude that LoRA does not present the best tradeoff for you.

It is also worth noting that even though LoRA does well on this task, we're not talking about vanilla LoRA. On one side, we have LoRA with rank stabilized initialization, which is a technique to scale the LoRA contribution differently from the default initialization and provides very good test accuracy (53.2%). On the other end, we have LoRA-FA, which uses an optimizer specialized for LoRA that freezes part of the LoRA weights and is thus more memory efficient (20.2 GB). Normal LoRA only achieves an accuracy of 48.1% at 22.5 GB memory and should thus be avoided in favor of the alternatives.

Next let's take a look at the image generation benchmark. In the Hugging Face Space, choose “image-gen” in the “Select Task” dropdown to show the results. The goal of the task is to learn a new concept, namely a cat plushy, and generalize it to new prompts.

For this task, the main metric is “dino similarity”, which measures how much a generated image resembles the picture from a holdout test dataset, with higher values being better. As always, we also want to keep an eye on memory usage. When plotting the Pareto Frontier of these two metrics, we find that LoRA is below that frontier. Let's get concrete numbers: LoRA achieves a similarity score of 0.697 whereas OFT achieves 0.708; in terms of memory, LoRA requires 9.97 GB, and OFT requires 9.01 GB. Therefore, OFT strictly dominates LoRA on these metrics.

Of course, you should also check the other PEFT methods that are close to the Pareto frontier, as metrics can be subject to small variations due to randomness. Also, you should explore other metrics: is runtime performance important to you or do you care about the size of the checkpoints? Choose the relevant metric from the dropdown and the picture can change considerably. For the image generation benchmark, do inspect the generated sample images to get a vibe of the fine-tuned model's capability.

Objection: But the benchmarks favor one method over another!

One criticism that could be leveled at the PEFT benchmarks is that the choice of hyper-parameters may favor one technique over another. This is true, doing an exhaustive and fair hyper-parameter sweep with this many techniques is difficult. It is, however, very easy for everyone to contribute their own experiments to PEFT: If you believe that a specific PEFT technique can be improved by choosing different hyper-parameters, create a PR! We added instructions on how to do that. In a similar vein, if you want to contribute a completely new benchmark, reach out to us to discuss your idea.

Another problem with the benchmarks is that they may not fully reflect the capabilities of a specific PEFT technique. We make it possible to compare the techniques along many different dimensions and discover the best ones according to these tradeoffs. But it's impossible to capture all facets this way. For instance, one PEFT technique called Cartridges was developed to compress long prompts, which is not measured in the benchmarks. Other factors can also influence the choice, for instance:

The benchmarks cannot fully lift the responsibility to do your research, but they can be reasonable pointers.

Objection: But llama.cpp/vLLM/... only supports LoRA

A limitation of using a PEFT technique other than LoRA is that they don't get the broad support in downstream packages that LoRA sees. For example, if you want to serve the model using vLLM, only LoRA checkpoints can be loaded. Thankfully, PEFT now supports converting other adapters into LoRA. That way, you can convert a non-LoRA checkpoint into LoRA and use it in vLLM or other downstream packages.

To test this, we converted an image adapter using the GraLoRA technique into a LoRA checkpoint. The test scores were virtually identical after conversion (similarity 0.702 → 0.694, 0.260 → 0.269). Below are test images for the prompt “sks cat at the beach”:

At the moment, we haven't implemented conversion for all PEFT techniques, but if there is demand, we will expand the support.

While working on the PEFT package, we noticed that LoRA has a lot of momentum behind it, even though other PEFT techniques are potentially better. Therefore, we set out to add benchmarks to PEFT that could paint a more objective picture of how well different PEFT techniques perform on different metrics.

Given the results we found, we can confidently conclude that LoRA is not a bad choice at all, but there are potentially better choices. Especially when checking the image generation benchmark, LoRA is beaten by other techniques. We discussed that besides metrics, other considerations must be taken into account when choosing the right PEFT technique. However, even then, we are pushing PEFT further to achieve feature parity between LoRA and those other techniques.

Our journey is far from finished; we want to extend and improve the existing benchmarks, and we also plan to add more benchmarks in the future. We ensured that it is easy for the community to contribute, so if this is something you would like to do, please open an issue on the PEFT repository and let us know how you would like to contribute.

If you take away only one thing from this article, it is that LoRA should not be the automatic default when choosing a PEFT technique for your use case. Given the unified API provided by PEFT, changing from one PEFT technique to another is as easy as switching one config in your code. And even if you stick with LoRA, check out all the variants that are supported in PEFT: DoRA, rs-LoRA, LoRA-FA etc. Give these other techniques a try and you might be pleasantly surprised.

Example: Changing from LoRA to OFT using PEFT:

What about DEFT?It adapts a pre-trained weight matrix by decomposing its update into two components with two trainable matrices: (1) a projection onto the complement of a low-rank subspace spanned by a low-rank matrix, and (2) a low-rank update. The single trainable low-rank matrix defines the subspace, while the other trainable low-rank matrix enables flexible parameter adaptation within that subspace.

Was there a reason EMLoC and the Drag-and-Drop LLMs methods weren't included in the comparison?

We only included techniques that are implemented in PEFT, and those two are not implemented.

#10154. Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.)

Viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each new word from reshuffling the paragraph.

hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

The first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

Underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

Variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

Light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

Mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

Numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

The tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

The quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

Default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

:where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

:is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

Here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

Browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

Some of these rules are still too new for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

"English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention,"

"English nests double quotes inside single quotes, American English reverses that convention (like it usually does),"

It’s nowhere near that cut-and-dried, and double has historically and geographically been much more popular. For some reason, UK publishing mostly switched to single for the 1900s, but they seem to be returning to double these days. Very few other countries followed them to single—Canada and Australia, for example, stuck with double.

A couple of links to start with (and you can find plenty more elsewhere): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotation_mark#In_English, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotation_marks_in_English#Quotations_and_speech

Overall, :lang(en) double-first with :lang(en-GB) single-first is a decent balance. If you had :lang(en) single-first, you’d want :lang(en-US, en-CA, en-IN, en-AU, en-NZ, …) for double-first.

A more accurate wording of the first sentence would be:

Quote style and character order differ by locale and house style.

I don’t understand the reason to use font-synthesis: none;. Isn’t synthesis just a fallback for when the author makes a mistake with the font faces or when the font file doesn’t load? Users’ fallback font-families likely have weight and style variants but probably not small-caps, maybe it at least should be allowed to be synthesized.

Instead of max-width: 65ch; being applied to p, li, dd, I’d consider applying it to p, dl, ol, ul. Limiting the width of the lists, rather than the list items, prevents longer items from “sticking out” relative to the paragraphs above and below, do to the items’ inline-start margins, padding.

The browser should automatically use French-style quotes (« ») within lang=fr; appears the British quote convention is not automatically used when lang=en-GB, at least not on my USian computer.

It might be worth noting more clearly that some of these are experimental/straight up don’t work today.

hanging-punctuation is Safari-only and doesn’t seem to support quotation marks in my testing, so the text is perhaps inaccurate on that point? Many of the hyphenation properties also only work in Safari, and require the prefixes described as “legacy” in the article.

It’s mentioned briefly in the intro that some stuff is experimental, but being more explicit in the sections about what does/doesn’t work currently would be great.

Definitely cool to explore the upcoming features, but feels a bit odd to frame it as a “reset” when it will likely change how text looks in the future in untested/unexpected ways, and includes superfluous code that won’t actually impact rendering today.

Limiting body, p, li and dd width is not the job of a reset. That’s a per-site choice and should be with other per-site css, not part of a reset block. And there’s lot’s of other very opinionated stuff as well. I’ll stick with my old friend Eric Meyer.

-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased; is contentious (ill-advised); text-rendering: optimizeLegibility; is unwarranted; font-synthesis: none; has implications the typical user may not realise or like (though avoiding the need for synthesis is definitely preferable); font-size-adjust: from-font; has problematic side-effects, trading one problem for another that is in my opinion at least as bad; text-box is not widely supported and has layout implications that mean your layout will be somewhat broken in other browsers; Given the preceding ruleset, [contenteditable="true"] { text-wrap: stable; } doesn’t work if the content is within an inner p, li, dd (which it typically will be); Hyphenation is just all-round dodgy and generally better avoided; Hanging punctuation is contentious and current implementations are really not very pleasing; Turning contextual alternatives on generally is not necessarily a good idea—there’s a reason it’s opt-in and separated from the normal set of ligatures; font-kerning: normal; is ill-advised: let the browser decide, if it decides not to do kerning, it’ll be for a good reason; font-variant-position: [sub|super]; is a terrible idea when combined with font-synthesis: none, because you can’t know what font the text will be rendered in (no, your web font is not guaranteed to work; more people than you might realise block them and/or force the use of their own chosen fonts—I for one, it makes the web so much better), and the fallback font is unlikely to support the feature; and finally, :is(h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6), p, blockquote, figcaption, li is a completely useless example of :is().

Thank you for gathering these typography rules into one tidy reset — the section on font-size-adjust stood out to me, as fallback fonts so often change the apparent size of a page while a webfont loads. I also appreciated the honest note that text-box-trim and hanging punctuation are still unevenly supported, so the guardrails matter as much as the declarations themselves. It is a genuinely useful starting point that I will try on a small project first.

A reset that handles fluid type and vertical rhythm together is the part most resets skip. Hyphens in the same file is a nice touch.

I'd test the trimmed text beside an SVG icon with the webfont blocked, especially when the label wraps.

Thank you for pulling all of this together into tidy-typography.css, Stu. The section I keep coming back to is the one on rendering and fallback sanity. I spend a lot of time previewing font pairings, and the fallback swap is exactly where most sites lose their rhythm — a display face loads, the fallback is visibly narrower or taller, and the whole layout jumps. Your point about font-size-adjust: from-font reducing that apparent size change while a webfont swaps in is the clearest explanation of that fix I have read, and pairing it with font-synthesis: none so the browser does not invent a bold or italic face the family does not actually have makes the reset feel considered rather than just defensive.

The fluid typography section was the most useful part for me in practice. Using container query units so a heading scales to the column it occupies, instead of clamp() with vw scaling it as though it were always in a full-width article, solves a real problem I hit constantly: the same heading in a 300px sidebar should not behave like the same heading in the main column. The same goes for text-wrap: pretty and text-wrap: balance replacing the JavaScript orphan fixers I used to reach for, and the hyphenation tuning with hyphenate-limit-chars and hyphenate-limit-lines — I had never thought carefully about the ladder effect of several hyphenated lines in a row until this article. I also appreciated the honest framing that text-box-trim and hanging-punctuation are still unevenly supported, so they need @supports guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

One practical habit from my own work that fits well with this reset: when I test a new pairing, I preview it at small sizes with font-optical-sizing: auto on, because a face that looks crisp at display size can turn thin and hard to read at body size, and I check the same text with the webfont blocked so I can see the fallback in isolation. For anyone who wants a quick place to try out different styles side by side while testing a pairing, I keep a handy reference at https://fontsgenerators.net/ — it is useful for seeing how a style holds up before committing it to a stylesheet like this one. I will be trying tidy-typography.css as a base on my next project and keeping the experimental declarations behind @supports, exactly as you suggest.

#10152. Build full-stack Android apps with Gemini in Google AI Studio

Google AI Studio, with Gemini 4 Carbon and Hydrogen, now enables you to build and ship full-stack, Android applications and publish to the Play Store in minutes. You can now go from a single prompt to a production-ready Kotlin Android app complete with data persistence, user sign-in, and AI features. Simply bring your idea and the Google AI Studio Build agent takes care of the entire setup. From configuring your database to securely calling the Gemini API, you can rapidly build and test on your own device directly from the Play Store at no cost.

Alongside full-stack Firebase backend provisioning, a major wave of upgrades is rolling out across the Android development workflow in Google AI Studio. Developers can now iterate in a faster, high-definition (HD) Android emulator with real-time audio output, send one-click emulator screenshots directly to the coding agent for visual UI changes, and style apps with custom fonts.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Here is what is launching today for Android app development in Google AI Studio:

Previously, Android apps generated in AI Studio were limited to local session storage. Now, when your prompt describes an Android app that needs persistent storage, user sign-in, or generative AI features, the Google AI Studio Build agent proactively detects those requirements. With your confirmation, the agent provisions the backend and wires up your Kotlin codebase automatically:

Under the hood, the Build agent automatically adds the Firebase Bill of Materials (BoM) and generates clean, idiomatic Kotlin code for your data and AI layers:

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

Building great mobile interfaces requires a tight visual and interactive feedback loop. Both the in-browser Android emulator and the Build agent's toolchain include new capabilities to help you inspect, hear, and refine your app in real time:

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Testing in an emulator accelerates iteration, but nothing replaces running your app on a physical device. Historically, installing a newly built Android app onto a phone required enabling USB debugging cables, managing signing keystores locally, or setting up a full developer console account.

With Google Play integrated directly into Google AI Studio, you can set up a Play account in a few clicks from the publish panel and publish your app straight to your personal Google Play library. Google AI Studio builds and signs the Android App Bundle (.aab) behind the scenes, so you can immediately download and run your custom Android app on your phone directly from Google Play.

All of these features are rolling out in Google AI Studio today. To get started, open Google AI Studio Build, select the Android chip at the top of the workspace, and try one of these prompts:
