#10150. How AI-Powered Cameras Are Changing Content Creation: What Developers Should Know

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Creating high-quality visual content once meant specialized cameras, technical knowledge and hours of editing. Today, software does a growing share of that work. Cameras recognize subjects, adjust exposure, stabilize footage and hand clips to editing tools that transcribe, reframe and tag them.

Digital photography made images easy to capture, review and share. Smartphones then folded capture, editing and publishing into one device. The next shift was computational photography: instead of relying only on the lens and sensor, the device combines several captures and processes them in software.

High dynamic range (HDR) imaging is the clearest example. A camera captures frames at different exposures and merges them so both bright skies and dark foregrounds keep detail. Research indexed on PubMed, published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, examines how deep learning has advanced HDR imaging, particularly in reconstructing visual information across different exposure levels.

Machine learning extends this approach from merging pixels to understanding them, which is what lets a camera decide what is the subject and what is the background.

Most AI camera features fall into a few groups.

Because of these failure modes, a pipeline should check what the camera produced before running expensive downstream steps.

A cheap pre-check can reject a frame that is too soft or badly exposed before you spend time on transcription, upscaling or model inference. The script below uses numpy and Pillow. It measures sharpness as the variance of a Laplacian, a standard blur indicator, and measures exposure as the share of crushed and clipped pixels.

The test builds a detailed random frame and a blurred copy, then checks that the sharp frame scores far higher, that a mostly black frame is flagged as underexposed and that a mostly white frame is flagged as overexposed:

Run the tests with python3 test_frame_quality.py. In our run, the detailed test frame scored about 33,000 for sharpness and its blurred copy scored under 2.

Traditional capture means holding a camera, propping up a phone or setting up equipment. Wearable cameras let creators record from their own point of view while their hands stay free, which suits travel video, instructional content, outdoor activities and behind-the-scenes footage.

Camera-equipped smart glasses are one form of this. Several makers sell them, and consumer listings such as ai glasses with camera show how the category is presented to buyers. Depending on the device, users start recording with physical controls or voice commands. Specifications differ widely, so compare field of view, storage, battery life and software support before choosing one.

For developers, wearables change the input. Footage is shaky, framed by head movement and often recorded outdoors, which is exactly where a quality check and stabilization matter. Battery capacity, camera position, storage and recording duration also limit extended productions. Wearables are an additional option for perspectives that are hard to reach otherwise, not a replacement for traditional cameras.

Editing involves reviewing clips, correcting color, adjusting audio and preparing videos for each platform. AI tools automate several repetitive parts of that work:

Creative judgment stays human. Choosing meaningful moments, shaping narrative flow and keeping a consistent visual style are decisions software cannot reliably make. Real-time assistance during recording will depend on hardware, software and environmental conditions.

As cameras get smaller, responsible recording matters more. Wearable devices can capture footage without the obvious movements of a handheld camera, so people nearby may not know recording is happening. The European Data Protection Board has highlighted transparency, personal data protection and recording awareness as important considerations for camera-equipped smart glasses.

Authenticity is the second challenge. AI tools can enhance an image, but heavy alteration can also mislead. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has examined technical approaches to digital content transparency, including provenance tracking, watermarking and synthetic-content detection. On the provenance side, the C2PA coalition publishes an open standard called Content Credentials, which helps show where content came from and what edits it has undergone.

Cameras will likely get better at faster subject recognition, more efficient automated editing and stronger low-light performance as computer vision and on-device computing advance. Wearables may widen first-person storytelling, and editing tools may make multi-platform publishing simpler. Technical gains alone will not decide quality, though. Originality, storytelling and thoughtful creative decisions still do.

Not always. Toolkits such as ML Kit face detection and Apple's Vision framework run image analysis on the device, which reduces delay and keeps frames local.

It narrows the gap in many conditions, but optics, sensor size and control still matter for demanding work, and AI enhancement can introduce artifacts of its own.

Add an early quality gate that checks sharpness and exposure, as in the script above, and calibrate its thresholds on your own footage.

It depends on location and context. Regulators such as the European Data Protection Board have raised transparency and consent concerns, so check local rules and be open about recording.

Provenance standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to show a file's origin and edit history, though they only help when tools and platforms support them.

#10149. MosaicLeaks: Can your research agent keep a secret?

A research agent at a healthcare firm is working through a routine question, and along the way it fires off a handful of ordinary-looking web searches. One references a cloud-migration milestone, one a January 2024 security disclosure, one narrows down which vendor got hit. No single query necessarily gives away the whole secret. But anyone watching the agent's outbound traffic can reassemble the fragments: MediConn had migrated 70% of its infrastructure to the cloud by January 2025, a fact that lived only in private documents. This is the mosaic effect, and it's the failure mode at the centre of MosaicLeaks.

MosaicLeaks treats those web queries as the leakage channel: the adversary never sees the private documents or the agent's reasoning, only the cumulative query log, and tries to infer private enterprise information from it.

We measure leakage in three ways, depending on what the adversary can infer from the observed queries:

These three represent increasing levels of concern. Intent leakage reveals what the agent is investigating. Answer leakage means the query log holds enough to answer a private question someone already has in hand. Full-information leakage is the strongest case: the observer can discover and state private facts without being told what to look for.

How the mosaic effect drives MosaicLeaks's three leakage measures: Intent (predict the research questions), Answer (answer given questions about the private documents), and Full-Information (state verifiably true private claims). Here the agent searches twice about Lee's Market's 2020 traffic growth, leaking its intent, then issues a third query to answer a follow-up. Each query looks benign alone, but seen together they let an observer deduce that the answer was 15%, and so claim that Lee's online traffic grew 15% in 2020.

Each chain interleaves local and web sub-questions. The answer to one sub-question becomes a bridge entity in the next, so the agent must retrieve local information before it can form the next useful web query. Local documents come from DRBench-style enterprise tasks, and web documents come from BrowseComp-Plus. The final split contains 559 training chains, 98 validation chains, and 344 held-out-company test chains.

The final web hop doesn't inherently contain any private information and can be answered from public web documents. However, because the path to it depends on private local facts, a query that carries forward "MediConn", "70%", and "January" gives the adversary enough context to recover internal information.

We use a simplified agent harness adapted from DRBench. The model answers each sub-question with a short answer and justification, allowing us to evaluate each hop individually with normalized string matching.

At each iteration, the model can use four tools. Plan produces local and web search queries, which are executed and returned as document cards. Choose selects which retrieved documents to read. Read attempts to answer the current hop from each selected document in parallel. Resolve decides whether to answer, read more documents, or plan another search.

One agent rollout. Each row is a hop, labeled local (L) or web (W) with its accepted answer. The colored blocks show the wall-clock time spent planning, retrieving, choosing, reading, and resolving that hop.

The obvious fix is to just ask. Add a line to the Plan prompt telling the agent not to issue web queries that leak local information, and see what happens to performance, leakage, and query behavior.

The prompt helps slightly for some models, but its effect is inconsistent and significant leakage remains. It also often has a negative effect on task performance. For Qwen3-4B, the prompt lowers answer/full-information leakage from 34.0% to 25.5%, but strict chain success drops from 48.7% to 44.5%. The primary behavioral change appears to be fewer web queries, not consistently safer query construction.

The first is a situational task reward. A single research trajectory can run to dozens of model calls, so giving them all the same final trajectory score is very weak credit: a successful run can reinforce a leaky search, and a failed run can punish a locally sound decision. Instead, we judge each call against other calls made at the same stage and hop, with the same information available. A Plan call is rewarded for searching the correct source and retrieving the right document; if that document is already in hand, it is rewarded for not searching again. A Choose call is rewarded for selecting the document that holds the answer. We train these stages because their desired behavior can be checked directly.

Task-only RL improves research performance but increases leakage. PA-DR keeps almost all of the performance gain while sharply reducing it.

And it did not get safer by simply searching less. PA-DR actually issues more web queries than the base model, but those queries drop the revealing details: specific metrics like "15%" or "2024", and clues about the kind of answer it is looking for. The agent still finds the right public documents. It just stops carrying private fragments along in the query text.

Training efficiency. The final column is how many generated samples each method needs to reach ~55% strict chain success. Lower is better.

Situational rewards reach outcome-reward-level task success using roughly 5-6x fewer generated samples. PA-DR keeps the sample-efficiency benefit while sharply reducing leakage.

MosaicLeaks is a controlled benchmark, not a measurement of leakage in deployed systems. The enterprise documents are synthetic, the web corpus is fixed, the chains span three company contexts, and every result comes from a single agent harness running multi-hop question answering rather than open-ended research. That control is what makes leakage measurable hop by hop, but broader tasks, real deployments, and other agent designs still need their own study.

Fascinating work on the mosaic effect. It makes me wonder how PA-DR holds up when agents are deployed for active threat intelligence or software auditing. For instance, if an enterprise research agent is tasked with analyzing potential security vectors or reverse-engineering third-party mobile apps from repositories like https://toemodapk.com, its web-query logs could easily leak proprietary internal app versions or specific device compliance criteria to an outside observer. Teaching agents to scrub those granular technical identifiers during deep web retrieval is going to be massive for operational security.

#10145. We got local models to triage the OpenClaw repo for FREE!*

*Free as in beer, excluding the cost of electricity, and assuming you already own the hardware

June 2026 will go down as the moment that people realized closed models can be taken away. With the removal of Anthropic's latest flagship model Claude Fable 5 fresh in memory, one can see why it is more important than ever to own your AI stack and be able to run models locally, especially if you are building your business on top of AI.

In that light, we wanted to share how we use local models like Gemma and Qwen in an agent harness, to run classification tasks[1]. This approach is different from using a model like BERT for classification. A local model in an agent harness like Pi can be used in tandem with structured outputs, to assign labels. We chose this approach because we already had local models and the harness on hand, and have conviction that similar setups will increase in popularity as local models improve in capability.[2]

Our starting point was open source contributions in the OpenClaw repo. OpenClaw gets hundreds of issues and PRs every day, which need to be triaged, prioritized and routed to maintainers. I, Onur, am working to make local models work well with OpenClaw. Being a maintainer of this specific vertical, I need to react quickly to any P0 issues.

With SOTA closed models like GPT-5, Opus, or Sonnet, this is a pretty straightforward task. But I happen to sit on 128 GB of unified memory, namely an NVIDIA GB10. So I took on the task:

Can I build a real-time notification system that filters and notifies me for only the issues that I am responsible for... with local open-weight models?

If I set up my OpenClaw main agent running on a $200/mo ChatGPT Pro plan to trigger a job on every new issue or PR, that would use up my quota. I might instead set it to run every 2 hours, or 6 hours. This would batch issues over longer periods, so we would be trading real-time notifications for delayed processing.

If I were to run this on a local model on the hardware I already have up and running, I would not only have near-instantaneous notifications, I would also be able to do it for free (or rather, for the cost of electricity).

We came up with a finite set of labels representing the categories of issues we need to triage, and then use a local model to classify each issue into one of those categories, like local_models, self_hosted_inference, acp, agent_runtime, codex, ui_tui and so on.[3]

But how do we classify pull requests? A simple single request to a Chat Completions endpoint with a tool JSON schema, with the topics as an enum?

Kind of. But this is 2026, not 2023, and we have AGENTS. We can do better!

For the local model choices, we tested gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b. With performance optimizations, both can generate hundreds of tokens per second locally.

We use an agent harness to drive the classification run. For this, we bundle pi as a harness that can call local model endpoints.

The agent by default receives the PR title, body and a truncated excerpt of the PR diff in the first prompt. Then, it can choose to use the bash tool to perform read-only operations on the OpenClaw repo (in case it needs to look at the codebase), or the final_json tool to submit the final classification result.

You wouldn't want to give full bash access to a local model running in this high-throughput setting, because a prompt-injected issue or PR could otherwise steer the model into doing something unrelated to classification.

For that reason, we use reposhell instead of bash: a restricted bash-like shell that only allows read-only operations (ls, find, cat, grep, etc.) on the OpenClaw repo. The model thinks it is using bash, but any operation that is not allowed is rejected:

Here is a concrete example where this mattered. In one saved session example, qwen3.6-35b-a3b was classifying openclaw/openclaw#84621, titled Fix Kimi tool-call rewriting stop reason handling. The thinking block shows the model initially considering coding_agent_integrations because the changed path extensions/kimi-coding made it look plausible. The model used reposhell to inspect the local repo with simple read-only commands like ls extensions, ls extensions/kimi-coding, and cat extensions/kimi-coding/package.json. That package metadata showed the extension was actually @openclaw/kimi-provider, an OpenClaw Kimi provider plugin. So the model corrected the final labels to inference_api and tool_calling, and explicitly excluded coding_agent_integrations.

We have mentioned earlier that we bundle a specific pi configuration that can only perform read-only operations and return classification output. We call it localpager-agent, named after localpager, the main project here. Each PR and issue generates a prompt, which is then passed to the CLI like below, alongside other args:

So then what orchestrates everything in between the incoming PR/issue and the final notification on Discord?

The orchestration around this is very simple; only the classification step involves an LLM:

Below is a figure showing the overall architecture of localpager:

The architecture is semi-agentic. Labeling is done agentically, while sending a notification is handled by deterministic rules. This is to make the notification pipeline faster by removing the need for inference for the most straightforward parts of the task. Local inference is free but each task has a resource contention cost: GPU bandwidth should be reserved for tasks where inference is absolutely needed. This also reduces chance of errors from notification.

Let's be frank: the first local versions of this system were noisy. The first model tested - gemma-4-e4b-it was useful for getting the end-to-end local pipeline working, but it also had a tendency to put too many unrelated labels on a PR or issue. False positive labels make the Discord feed noisy and don't focus my attention on the right issues. That pushed us toward testing larger local models, including gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b, on the 330-row evaluation set below.

For early prompt work, we also used DeepSeek-V4-Flash through the antirez DS4 implementation[4] to create the earlier dataset labels. That setup used the DS4 server over CUDA. We eventually gave up on DS4 as the labeler because it was not labeling consistently across runs. We also did not consider it as the main localpager-agent model because it was too big to get enough throughput on our hardware: the DS4 server gave us around 14 tokens per second, with maximum concurrency of 1.

To test model performance, we selected and generated labels for 330 GitHub issues and PRs. Each item was labelled five times (3x GPT-5.5 and 2x Opus 4.8) with the models needing to be in agreement to be accepted. This process involved hand adjudicating, improving label definitions and highlighting internal product design choices for the models. This gave us a set of stable, reproducible labels to compare our smaller models against.

We did not need to do prompt optimization for gemma-4-26b-a4b or qwen3.6-35b-a3b before getting useful results on this evaluation set. Using the same routing prompt, Gemma had higher recall and lower wall-clock time per row, while Qwen had higher precision, higher exact match, and fewer false positives. We also ran DeepSeek-V4-Flash on the same set as a reference. It had the fewest false positives, but the model size and throughput make it impractical for executing these tasks in real time on the NVIDIA GB10. Since each row can have multiple labels, false positives and false negatives are total label counts across all rows. The Qwen results below are after retrying structured-output failures where the model ran out of output tokens before calling final_json. For Gemma and Qwen, repeated-run metrics report mean ± sample standard deviation across three runs. DeepSeek-V4-Flash was run once as a reference.

The throughput and wall-clock numbers here are not definitive maximum performance numbers for these models on this hardware. They are the settings we used at the time with the optimizations we had available. For example, in a separate probe, gemma-4-26b-a4b also supported concurrency 32 and reached over 700 aggregate output tokens per second.

For the Gemma benchmark, we served gemma-4-26b-a4b with vLLM using the optimizations we found available for this setup. A big part of that is the NVFP4 quantization: on GB10-class Blackwell hardware, it is not just a smaller model file, but a hardware-friendly format that can use the NVIDIA/vLLM execution path more directly than a portable GGUF quantization like Q4_K_M. In practice, that means less memory traffic and more room for batching. We also enabled prefix caching, FP8 KV cache, the CUTLASS MoE backend, and language-model-only mode. The full 330-row run finished in about 7.5 minutes at concurrency 16.

We have mentioned earlier that instead of running a job with a local model for every new issue or PR, we can run a batch job with a SOTA cloud model, like GPT-5.5 running in OpenClaw, every n hours (e.g. every 2 hours) to achieve the same end.[5]

In that case, we would need a ChatGPT Pro plan. Since the model is SOTA, we can still expect it to perform reasonably well, despite batching 2 hours of issues/PRs together.

Because we want to see how well the local classifier performs against GPT-5.5, we run both simultaneously, and let GPT-5.5 be the judge of false positives and negatives, every 2 hours.

To be safe, we run the OpenClaw job in a sandbox, with only access to the public repo we report results to. In our case, we let the OpenClaw job update a machine-readable file, then a simple script reads the Codex-assigned labels and computes the false positive/negative status. Example output:

The instructions on how to classify, edit the machine-readable file, get the false positives and false negatives using a script are present in an agent skill which is referenced in an OpenClaw cron job that runs every 2 hours. The OpenClaw agent then ingests any new issues or PRs, adds them to the JSON file with appropriate labels, runs the scripts and reports back in the same Discord channel. This way, we can observe the local model's performance every few hours, and get notified of the misses.

We think that the issue/PR triage task is a specific case of a broader set of tasks which we call "high throughput triage". This post explored the idea of using a local model to filter out information in real time in only one domain, that is, open source contributions. The ability of medium-sized local models like gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b to zero-shot classify with good accuracy without any need for fine-tuning makes them a good first choice for quick prototyping, before one moves on to more cost-efficient traditional classifier models.

However, the same approach can be applied to other domains as well:

The list can be extended, but we think that the idea should be clear.

Besides triaging, we have also explored how classification can be performed with agent harnesses running fast local models in a secure manner. A good naming for the approach would be agentic classification: the model is not fed the entire body of information upfront, but can search for more context before returning structured data. While we cannot exactly call this a novel approach, we hope for this blog post to be a good reference for the specific Pi+a restricted shell+final_json recipe.

#10144. CSS-Tricks, Version 20

I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago. That’s ancient in web (and dog) years.

It’s not like the site has simply sat all that time. We pushed lots of changes and shipped new features, particularly since 2024, but we never really got the paint brushes out of storage.

Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the new v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump.

Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why.

First and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust.

For example, the global compiled JavaScript file retained some scripts that just weren’t being used anymore. Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML

. There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. We had some scripts for serving third-party ads that are no longer needed now that we’re self-hosting ads. Things like that. The overall JavaScript was nicely trimmed from 151.6 KB (55.3 KB gzipped) to 133.8 KB (48.1 KB).

I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme.

There were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out.

Yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. I think we’re sporting a more modern workflow than before, even if there’s still room to grow. A smattering of the related commits:

For years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a new terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention quickly. Very happy here.

Oof, this is everyone’s favorite job, right?! Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. I prompted it to review recent WordPress security release notes and identify areas where the theme could be hardened to comply with what WordPress is doing.

Whoa, you used AI? Yeah, I sure did. But for things like this where it could be my little gopher and allow me more time to do what I do best: front-end. I’m still able to make most of the patches myself based on the output recommendations, but it’s nice to have a gut-check for things where I’m clearly no expert, like security.

I still use and like Sass very much. I mean, yes, I would like to be straight-up vanilla CSS everywhere, but I can’t tear myself away from partials in particular.

The previous theme had a fairly nice “flat” structure — very few partial directories and most things all in the same top-level source. Totally cool. But an organization nut like me (you should see my house) has to have a place for everything to live. It ain’t perfect, but I’m happy with what I was able to put together without leveling the building in the process.

There are some compromises. Like, /header should really be in /layout. The ordering is really important, though, and some of my ideals were simply not possible. I’m hoping to eventually work in some sort of Cascade Layers structure.

I’m pleased as punch to see the overall size of CSS drop in the process. It went from 180 KB (31.7 KB) to 169 KB (24.6 KB). Not hugely significant, but not not significant either. I had to do a couple tricky things to cheat my way there, like serving all the form styles I’m about to talk about into a separate forms.css file and serving it just on pages where WooCommerce, Restrict Content Pro, and Gravity Forms are enqueued.

Are you starting to notice a trend? We’re still talking about fairly invisible work. CSS-Tricks has so many nooks and crannies that it’s nearly impossible to make things perfectly consistent across the board. But because of those nooks and crannies, so many fixed values, magic numbers, one-off styles, and older utilities were hiding about. I decided to tackle a good chunk of that while reorganizing the Sass.

For example, there are now semantic design tokens that abstract away one-off colors. So many grays, let me tell you. Now there’s a maintainable palette that’s referenced throughout. Same with fonts, font styles, and font sizes. Same with paddings and margins. It feels a lot better to make a change at the “system” level with confidence that the change is taking effect everywhere it needs to.

But this is also where some clearly visible changes happened! Most notably, link styles are consistent all over the place with a small handful of intended and maintained variations. Not only is it more pleasing visually, but it improves accessibility throughout because the inherited styles default to proper visual cues that do not rely solely on color or opacity changes.

Oh, and my favorite piece of this? Forms and tables have both been redone. That’s tough to do in a WordPress theme where these components don’t always come from one source. For example, forms could come from any one of the Gravity Forms, WooCommerce, or Restrict Content Pro plugins, and they all have their own stylesheets. Resetting those allowed me to bring a certain level of harmony in all those instances.

OK, something even more visual. This is the first time CSS-Tricks has had more than one color scheme! It certainly could have been done a long time ago, but I’d also argue that the design hasn’t really called for a light/dark toggle over the last 8 years or so. It’s a nice blend of both light and dark elements that marry the best of both worlds no matter your theme preference.

But I had to take a stab, right? The site has predominantly been dark despite the content being against a white background, so I treated things as though a “dark” mode already existed. The result is a creamy light theme that is largely just a change in background and component styles. And I used some of what I learned from the recent “toggle” debate to handle system, dark, and light themes with a single toggle.

What hasn’t changed is the main content container you see in things like articles. That was already white, even in a “dark” mode, and I’m not confident that simply toggling it between white and black is the best approach. Something on the radar for sure.

Oh, and it’s all wired up to a view transition that slides the new theme over the previous one.

I hope you think the site’s header and footer are cute. Yes, cute. That’s what I was going for when adding a colorful series of dots as the backdrop.

Sorta like a subtle candy texture, right? Or a colorful group of stars? I dunno, but I’m calling it “Jawbreaker” for lack of a better term and because it reminds me of the jawbreaker candy I loved as a kid. Naming still sucks.

It’s all part of the same SVG. I really, really (really) wanted to random()-ly position dots around, but that would have taken a lot of empty individual elements (e.g., ) in the markup. Not my favorite. So, I generate the elements in PHP:

I really, really wanted to random()-ize all the things, but inlining random coordinates on each was the way to go. Same deal with the inlined styles that set a fill, and sizing for each circle in the texture, and variables that set a --delay and --dur on the subtle animation that twinkles them in and out.

I’ll have to look at generating the SVG using or whatever later since that pattern repeats in the footer, too.

That’s carried through to the 404 page as well:

If your browser supports border-shape and random() (only Chrome, I think), then the homepage gives you a blobby-blob shape behind the grid of author avatars. Hover it and it gets, you know, even blobbier.

It takes an existing pattern I’m calling .gradient-card:

…and sets a gradient on the component’s :before pseudo:

That sits underneath the :after pseudo that’s translucent, allowing the :before‘s gradient to show through a smidge:

The differing border-radius values allow :before to bleed outside, giving the impression of a border around the entire deal. That’s the basic shape. The border-shape is where things get blobby:

Those variables? They’re mapped to shape()s. I grabbed the first one from Temani Afif’s blob generator:

It’s called “static” because that’s the default state. Hover or focus on the component and it swaps out those points out with a “hover” version of the shape:

Those variables? They’re mapped to random() values:

So, the hover state is different on each page load. And we animate between the two:

I’m pretty stoked on this one. The Almanac has grown, evolved, and just plain gotten great the past few years. But the primary page for it… not so great. It was definitely overshadowed by work on the pages inside it and never revisited beyond clickable cards to get to each feature subset.

Now the page is a real index of the CSS features that gets you where you need to go quickly. Someone somewhere sometime did some sort of CSS periodic table. I forget where I’d seen that but the general idea sat with me and I thought I could pull it off. There’s nothing “tricky” about it but I love what the layout adds to the overall site.

This is another area that sorely needed love. Our guides have always been a vertical stack of items. The book effect was definitely cool, but I started believing that leaning on it as the main visual hook was holding things back from being more functional. With something like 27 guides, we’re talking about a lot of scrolling with no clear idea of what you’re going to see as you go.

Again, nothing “tricky” but I like the overall usefulness of the new layout. There’s a featured guide, a widget of newly added and updated guides, and a categorized grid of everything below that.

The pages that show all of an author’s published articles got a little spruce-up, too.

It’s a little change, really. The right sidebar was moved to the left and the author image and bio moved in, allowing the articles to creep up to the top. I hope to do more here since the small layout tweak opens up more opportunities.

Also need to do the larger Authors index, but another time.

This one’s just for those of us working in the WordPress editor. I don’t need a complete visual editor to get things done, but it is a nice affordance to have some of the front-end styles sneak into the editing UI for a better idea of what you’re working with.

Using Lighthouse to measure things like performance, accessibility, and best practices is woefully fraught with caveats, but there’s no reason to chuck it completely. I find them more fun than fact and I don’t mind the recommendations for improving things.

So, after a few runs and tweaks, here’s how things shook out theme-to-theme.

I’m happy here. There are some things I just don’t have the control to fix when it comes to performance, so seeing v20 come in consistent with v19 is just fine by me. I’m happier with the boosts to accessibility and best practices. SEO? Meh. Don’t really care unless it’s hurting more important things like accessibility.

Again, very happy. There’s little I can do with time to first byte but everything else seems to clock in at least marginally better. The total page weight is a clear win and that’s probably what I care most about here.

Oh gosh, there’s a lot more but they’re mostly minor things that don’t bubble up to the front end. Sort of the same way browser changelogs have some generic line of “bug squashing” or whatever. In this case, it’s things like better post queries and breadcrumbs and function management and naming and… you get it.

There’s definitely so much more to do. And plenty of things I’m sure I missed or broke along the way. That’s just life and those will have to come in another iterative release less worthy of a version bump. You can let me know what I muffed up in the comments.

I hope you at least like where this is going!

#10142. How to Build an Accessible Multi Step Form: A Practical Guide With a Vanilla JavaScript Example

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A long form can feel like a chore before anyone types a word. Splitting it into smaller steps lets people focus on a few related questions at a time.

The code looks simple: show one section, hide the rest and add a button. The difficult parts are validation, keyboard use, focus and what happens when JavaScript doesn't run. This guide builds an accessible multi step form with HTML and plain JavaScript. It also reproduces a bug that can leave visitors stuck on the first step.

Multiple steps make sense when questions fall into clear groups, such as project details, timing and contact information. A form with only an email address and a message usually doesn't need them.

Splitting a form doesn't make unnecessary questions useful. Remove those first. More steps also aren't a guarantee of more completed forms, so test the change with your own audience.

The W3C tutorial on multiple page forms advises dividing long forms into logical stages and telling users about their progress. Our example applies those ideas within a single page.

Without JavaScript, all three groups remain visible and Send works as an ordinary submit button. The Back button stays hidden because it has no job in that view. This approach is called progressive enhancement: start with a working form, then add the step behavior.

The action value is a placeholder. Point it to a real server endpoint in your project. If your stylesheet sets a display value on fieldsets, check that it doesn't override the hidden attribute.

Save the following code as form.js in the same folder:

The form has one submit button. Its label reads Continue until the last step. The submit handler decides whether to show an error, open the next step or let the browser send the data. Pressing Enter in a text field follows the same path.

Back is a regular button, so it never submits anything. The answers remain in their fields because the code only hides each step. It doesn't remove or rebuild it.

To test its purpose, I removed only this line, filled in the first field and pressed Enter in headless Chromium 158. The form stayed on step 1. The console reported messages like these:

Before firing the submit event, the browser checked the entire form. The empty required fields on later steps were invalid, but they were hidden. Submission was blocked, so our handler never had a chance to open step 2.

Setting noValidate stops that automatic check during submission. It doesn't disable checkValidity() or reportValidity(), so our code can validate only the visible step. Because the line lives in JavaScript, the browser's normal validation still applies if the script never loads.

For more detail on native validation rules and methods, see SitePoint's Complete Guide to HTML Forms and Constraint Validation.

The test intercepted the request, so it checked what the browser sent rather than a real server. It also doesn't show how other browsers behave.

Each legend includes the current step number, and the page title changes with it. After someone moves to another step, focus goes to the new legend. This gives keyboard users a clear starting point. The code doesn't move focus during the first page load.

The negative tabindex lets JavaScript focus a legend without adding it to the normal Tab order. Keep the focus outline visible, or replace it with an equally clear style. Screen reader behavior varies, so test with the browser and screen reader combinations your visitors use.

Native validation messages are useful for a small example. A production form may need persistent error text beside each field. If so, connect each message to its field with aria-describedby, set aria-invalid when needed and clear both after the error is fixed.

Also avoid asking for the same information twice. WCAG 2.2 Redundant Entry requires previously entered information needed again in the same process to be filled in or available to select. There are exceptions, including certain security needs and information that is no longer valid. This example alone doesn't make a whole website WCAG compliant.

Browser checks can be changed or bypassed. Your server should validate required fields, allowed choices, lengths and formats again. It should also handle spam, protect against cross site request forgery where relevant and escape stored values when displaying them.

Before release, try the complete form with only a keyboard. Check mobile layouts, zoom, browser autofill, Back and Forward navigation, slow connections and server errors. Make sure repeated clicks don't create duplicate records.

SitePoint's practical workflow for testing JavaScript forms is a helpful next step when you're preparing a broader test plan.

The example also leaves out conditional questions. If one answer can remove a later step, calculate the active steps before updating the progress label. Decide how to handle old answers from inactive branches, and enforce the same rules on the server.

Custom code gives you control over the markup and behavior, but your team must maintain validation, delivery, security and testing. A form builder can reduce the amount of interface code you manage. For example, LeadGen App lists multi step forms, conditional logic and website embedding among its features.

Whichever route you choose, test the finished form instead of relying on a feature list.

An accessible multi step form needs more than a few hidden sections. Start with semantic HTML, validate each visible step and keep progress and focus clear.

Pay special attention to required fields that appear later. A single hidden field can stop the first button from working, even when the visible answer is correct. Test that case, then check the whole journey with real users and a real server before launch.

#10141. PP-OCRv6 on Hugging Face: 50-Language OCR from 1.5M to 34.5M Parameters

Evaluate PP-OCRv6 online, then integrate lightweight, production-ready OCR with PaddlePaddle, Transformers, or ONNX Runtime backend.

PP-OCRv6 is the latest generation of PaddleOCR’s universal OCR model family. It is designed for real-world text detection and recognition across documents, screenshots, multilingual images, digital displays, industrial labels, and scene text.

The model family scales from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, with three tiers: tiny, small, and medium. The medium and small tiers support 50 languages, including Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages. Try PP-OCRv6 online quickly: PP-OCRv6 Online Demo.

On PaddleOCR’s official in-house multi-scenario OCR benchmarks, PP-OCRv6_medium reaches 86.2% detection Hmean and 83.2% recognition accuracy. Compared with PP-OCRv5_server, it improves text detection by +4.6 percentage points and text recognition by +5.1 percentage points.

PP-OCRv6 focuses on a practical OCR need: producing accurate, structured text outputs with small models and flexible deployment options. For a deeper discussion of why specialized OCR models remain useful in the VLM era, see our previous blog: PP-OCRv5 on Hugging Face: A Specialized Approach to OCR.

PP-OCRv6 introduces architecture, training, and data improvements across detection and recognition. The main design goal is to improve OCR accuracy while keeping model sizes suitable for different deployment settings.

PP-OCRv6 provides three model tiers, covering different model sizes and OCR accuracy levels.

PP-OCRv6 uses PPLCNetV4 as a unified backbone for text detection and text recognition.

For developers, the main benefit is consistency across the model family. The tiny, small, and medium tiers are not unrelated models; they are part of the same OCR family and share a common architectural direction.

Text detection is the first stage of the OCR pipeline. Detection quality affects the crops sent to the recognizer, and poor crops often lead to poorer recognition.

PP-OCRv6 upgrades the detection module with RepLKFPN, a lightweight large-kernel feature pyramid network designed for multi-scale text detection while keeping inference efficient.

This is relevant for real-world OCR inputs, where text may be small, dense, rotated, low-resolution, or embedded in complex backgrounds.

For text recognition, PP-OCRv6 uses EncoderWithLightSVTR. It combines local context modeling with global attention to improve recognition quality on challenging text crops.

The recognition improvements are especially relevant for multilingual text, screen text, industrial characters, special symbols, dense text, and noisy image regions.

The medium and small tiers support 50 languages in one model family, covering Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages.

This helps reduce the need for separate OCR models across common multilingual OCR scenarios.

Run OCR with Paddle Infernece(Default backend):

The OCR result can be saved as visualization images and structured JSON output. The structured output can then be used by downstream systems such as document parsing, search, extraction, RAG, analytics, or agent workflows.

PP-OCRv6 can be used with multiple inference backends through PaddleOCR. PaddleOCR 3.7 provides a unified inference-engine interface, where engine selects the underlying runtime and related configuration can be passed through the pipeline or module API.

For Hugging Face users, PaddleOCR supports running selected OCR and document parsing models with a Transformers backend. This can be enabled with:

For more details on how the Transformers backend works in PaddleOCR, see:

PaddleOCR: Running OCR and Document Parsing Tasks with a Transformers Backend

Run PP-OCRv6 example with Transformer Backend:

ONNX variants are also available in the PP-OCRv6 Collection for environments that use ONNX Runtime through engine="onnxruntime":

Together, these backend options make PP-OCRv6 available across different runtime environments while keeping the same OCR model family on the Hugging Face Hub.

PP-OCRv6 extends PaddleOCR with a lightweight, multilingual OCR model family for real-world text detection and recognition.

The release includes three model tiers from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, up to 50-language OCR support, improved detection and recognition accuracy over PP-OCRv5_server, and multiple model formats on the Hugging Face Hub, including safetensors, Paddle inference models, and ONNX models.

Together with the hosted Hugging Face Space and the available PaddleOCR inference backends, PP-OCRv6 provides several entry points for evaluation and integration:

Transformers Backend Blog: PaddleOCR with Transformers Backend

PaddleOCR Official Website: https://www.paddleocr.com

#10139. CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today?

CSS optimization is a deceptive topic. On the one hand, it feels like something simple that we should already have all the tooling for — especially when it comes to minification. On the other hand, the idea that we already exploited “everything” there is around CSS optimization may be considered naive. Such a claim looks hard to defend for a language that evolves almost daily.

In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO, or “using declarations just once.”

Aware of an older source? Please comment!

The technique is inspired by the principle of DRY, “don’t repeat yourself”, in that it works by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) declaration repetition.

So, if there’s something like display: flex and it appears two or more times, it gets reconciled in one rule:

The outcome of the technique depends on how intelligently the deduplication is done and how long the selectors are. Intelligence determines if UDJO leads to an actual maintainability advantage — can the change of a declaration really be done to all the selectors attached? And the selector length influences how big file size savings are.

If you’re interested, my article on “DRY CSS” describes the mechanics in more detail. The question here is: Is UDJO still effective and still relevant today?

When we try to answer this question, however, we end up with a problem: When sites are complex and their style sheet declarations have not been de-duplicated before, UDJO can require a lot of work.

To save some time, I built tooling for this work. While it didn’t seem like it would immediately be as comprehensive as manually going through and testing style sheets, it seemed realistic enough that a tool could catch some repetition.

Skipping ahead, I created CSS Dedup not only to identify repetition, but also to deduplicate what could safely be optimized (CSS Dedup has some documentation on this but in essence, deduplication affects selector locations, which is part of how the cascade works). This, then, gives us some data:

For the first batch, I arbitrarily picked 20 websites to analyze. I then used CSS Dedup to check what the file size changes would be if we deduplicated what seemed provably safe, and also what seemed probably safe, but only if it led to file size savings.

I picked those two options to provide the “natural” result of deduplication, but also the one site owners may be most interested in to reduce repetition but also decrease transfer size. After all, UDJO as a CSS optimization technique can improve both maintainability and performance.

Important note: These values cannot be used to tell CSS quality—they depend on selector length and also on verifying if deduplication, in the respective case, actually leads to better maintainability. Also note that this leaves out changes after compression—this was not part of the experiment but would be fair to test, too.

For the question whether UDJO still works today, this should be a yes. It works as well as to even come with file size savings.

Maybe you’re curious, too, about what the situation looks like in our field, among web developers. Let’s take some samples on this, too.

It would be valuable to expand this analysis to take more samples and investigate the differences across samples, but there may be something to web professionals using shorter selectors so as to be able to benefit more from UDJO.

As mentioned at the beginning, UDJO’s effectiveness generally depends on the kind of repetition as well as on the length of selectors.

This can be managed, however: While tools like CSS Dedup make no difference between declaration use cases (and are therefore blunt), it is possible to configure them so as to reap the performance benefits.

As the data taken for this article suggest, file size savings may be achieved in most cases. Considering that this is based on safe changes, this means a low-cost performance optimization vector — especially when applied to minified output. It’s still a good idea to couch that against the use of further compression (e.g. gzip/Brotli), but at face value, deduplication shows how it can reduce the size of CSS.

For anyone generally interested in CSS optimization, maintainability, and performance, UDJO should probably be part of the overall approach to CSS. But since the technique has been niche and since tooling is new, I invite you to review, test, and explore this vector. It seems hard to argue that we have reached the ceiling of how far we can take CSS optimization.

Andy Clarke shows you how to create designs that people recognize and remember in his brand-new e-book, Standout Designs for the Web. Order it today!

and also to add that in the last weeks I’ve been testing some approaches to using CSS Dedup. It has proven quite effective, especially in the following setup: On static sites, reaping only savings via css-dedup CSS_FOLDER -p "(?

I’ll write more about this shortly (on my website)—and am curious about your thoughts and observations!

I’d be curious to see the minuscule performance implications, if any at all.

If up to 11% savings in a small sample are true – even pre-compression – then that’s not minuscule. Especially not with the average size of a stylesheet.

I’d like to see more sites being tested both pre and post compression.

#10137. Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText

Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

DiLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

The Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This issue is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

In multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

Streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

Worked Example (Qwen3-32B in bfloat16, tstep​≈6.2s, P=H=65):

To evaluate distributed efficiency under realistic network bottlenecks, we benchmarked Qwen3-32B (64 decoder layers, partitioned into P = 65 fragments with H = 65) across 2× TPU v5p-32 slices (dcn_diloco_parallelism=2) using built-in Linux traffic-control (tc) bandwidth shaping to limit inter-slice bandwidth across three network regimes: Unthrottled (Line Rate), 30 Gbit/s aggregate (Moderate Congestion), and 10 Gbit/s aggregate (Severe Congestion).

A common question with low-communication training is whether allowing learners to train independently between synchronizations degrades model quality—especially on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, where independent updates could cause expert routers to drift apart.

We evaluated Streaming DiLoCo against synchronous Data Parallel pre-training across two MoE architectures in MaxText (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Gemma4-26B-A4B) over 4,000 training steps:

Empirical results confirm that Streaming DiLoCo preserves—and even slightly improves—validation loss:

MaxText provides a native JAX and Flax NNX implementation of both Vanilla and Streaming DiLoCo—requiring no external central parameter servers.

You can enable Streaming DiLoCo in your MaxText YAML configuration or CLI overrides by setting enable_diloco: true and enable_streaming_diloco: true. As a best practice, set both num_diloco_fragments (P) and diloco_sync_period (H) to N_layers + 1 so that exactly one fragment is synchronized per training step (Δh = 1):

In MaxText, diloco.py splits each global batch across the M learners so each learner processes GBS / M tokens per step. To overlap cross-slice communication with TPU computation in Streaming DiLoCo, weight deltas for the scheduled fragment are offloaded to M-way sharded syncer workers running on the learner host CPUs. Rather than routing through a single central coordinator, the host-CPU syncer shards execute a distributed all-reduce across the network in the background to average the fragment deltas while the TPUs continue running inner-loop training steps. Each syncer shard then applies the outer Nesterov momentum update locally and writes the updated fragment weights back to its colocated TPU learner. To dive deeper or launch your first run:

Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText decouples large-scale LLM pre-training from the requirement of a single, monolithic, high-bandwidth fabric. By combining use of an inner and outer optimizer with fine-grained parameter streaming, engineering teams can pool TPU slices across congested datacenter networks or geographically distributed metros—sustaining high hardware utilization without compromising model convergence. Streaming DiLoCo is available today in MaxText v0.2.5 on PyPI, the corresponding Docker images and on GitHub main. Try it today for experimenting with distributed training workloads.

#10135. Experimenting with the proposed Cross-Origin Storage API in Transformers.js

(This is a guest post by Developer Relations Engineer Thomas Steiner from the Chrome team at Google.)

Transformers.js provides Web developers with a simple way to use the power of transformers in their Web apps through task-specific pipelines. To run inference in the browser, developers create an instance of pipeline() and specify a task they want to use the pipeline for. As a concrete example, the following snippet shows how to set up an automatic speech recognition (ASR) pipeline.

You will notice in the source code that I specified Xenova/whisper-tiny.en as the model, which is a very decent choice for common English automatic speech recognition tasks. In fact, it's even the default model according to the Transformers.js default model resolution, as per the linked excerpt.

When you run this example in the browser, Transformers.js automatically takes care of downloading and caching the relevant model resources and Wasm files. The following screenshot shows the Chrome DevTools Cache storage section after visiting the app. When you reload the page, the resources are served from the Cache API, and the model returns results almost instantly.

However, Xenova/whisper-tiny.en being a popular model (and, as mentioned before, even being the ASR default model in Transformers.js), you can well imagine that more than just one app that you visit would use it. To simulate this situation, here's the same example app from before, but served from a different origin. When you visit this different origin app, rather than being usable almost instantly, the browser instead has to download and cache all the model resources again, even if they're byte-by-byte the same as before. Even in this toy example, this adds up to 177 MB of duplicate download and storage, as you can examine in the Storage section of the Chrome DevTools Application panel. You can imagine that this quickly adds up.

But it gets worse. Let's add a second pipeline to the toy example: sentiment analysis. Sentiment analysis by default uses the Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english model. By not specifying the model, Transformers.js' default model resolution automatically picks it for you.

Two entirely different AI models, but they depend on the same 4,733 kB ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm WebAssembly (Wasm) runtime file from the underlying ONNX Runtime library that Transformers.js is built on top of. Open the extended demo on a different origin, and you will notice in the Network tab how also the Wasm runtime gets downloaded and cached again.

So even if you run apps that don't share the same AI models, your browser still makes redundant requests for shared Wasm resources you already have, and on top of that also caches them again, which consumes space on your hard disk.

By default, AI model resources come from the Hugging Face Hub, and ultimately the Hugging Face CDN. The browser makes a request for a resource like https://huggingface.co/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/resolve/main/config.json which then gets redirected to the final CDN URL like https://huggingface.co/api/resolve-cache/models/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/0b6928efcb76139cae2c6881d49cda67fe119f42/config.json?%2FXenova%2Fdistilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english%2Fresolve%2Fmain%2Fconfig.json=&etag=%223c36342ef1f74de2797d667c68c6b7b988d0b87c%22 in this case.

The Wasm runtime resources are served from the jsDelivr CDN by default. For example, ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm comes from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm at the time of this writing.

The concrete implementation may vary by browser, but in Chrome, cached resources are keyed using a Network Isolation Key in addition to the resource URL. The Network Isolation Key is composed of the top-level site and the current-frame site. Take the previous toy examples hosted on the origins https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. If they both use the Wasm runtime from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm, their cache keys will look like in the following table.

So even if the resource URLs are exactly the same, since the Network Isolation Keys don't match, there's no cache hit, which means duplicate download and duplicate storage. This is the challenge that the Cross-Origin Storage proposal aims to tackle.

💡 Note: The Cross-Origin Storage API is an early-stage proposal that isn't final. While the proposed API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow.

The proposed Cross-Origin Storage (COS) API introduces a dedicated navigator.crossOriginStorage interface through which web apps can store and retrieve large files across origin boundaries, identified not by a URL, but by a cryptographic hash.

That last point about cryptographic hashes is key. Because COS identifies files by their hash rather than by their URL or origin, the same ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm Wasm runtime you downloaded while visiting https://googlechrome.github.io is recognized as identical to the one https://rawcdn.rawgit.net is about to request, no matter where either of the two origins fetched it from. See the following code snippet that illustrates the basic flow.

If the resource is in COS, you get back a FileSystemFileHandle from which you can read the blob directly via getFile() (the resulting File inherits from Blob). If the resource is not in COS, you fall back to the network, and write the resource into COS for the next app that needs it, which could be your app, or another unrelated app, potentially on a completely different origin.

The API is deliberately shaped after the File System Standard's FileSystemDirectoryHandle.getFileHandle() you likely are familiar with from the Origin Private File System (OPFS) API. The hash parameter plays the same role as the name parameter in OPFS: uniquely identifying a resource. The options.create flag works the same way: absent or false for read-only access, true when you intend to write.

Not every resource should be globally shared. COS gives developers precise control over visibility through the origins option when storing a file.

One important rule: visibility can be upgraded but never downgraded. If a file is already globally available, a later attempt to store it with a restricted origins list is silently ignored. This prevents a malicious actor from re-storing a public resource and narrowing its availability. The reverse is possible: a file initially stored with a restricted origins list can later be made more permissive. Any site, not just the original storer, can call getFileHandle() for the same hash (hashes are not a secret) with create: true and a broader origins value, and given the browser verifies the hash matches, the resource becomes available to the wider audience from that point on. Note that the upgrading site must still write the full file through the returned handle. This requirement exists to prevent sites from exploiting the upgrade path as a side-channel to detect whether a particular file was already stored in COS.

A subtle but important property of COS is that the browser verifies the hash when you write a file. If the data you write doesn't match the declared hash, the write fails with an error. This makes integrity checking automatic: an app reading a file from COS can be confident it's getting exactly the bytes it expected. The same guarantee it would have had if it had computed the hash itself after a network download.

This turns out to be doubly useful in the Transformers.js scenario. Today, after downloading model weights, most apps have no practical way to verify that the CDN served the right bytes. With COS, every file in the store is implicitly verified on write, no matter where it came from, the official Hugging Face CDN or a random site's self-hosted mirror.

Of course a cross-origin shared cache raises the same question as the partitioned HTTP cache in reverse: if any site can probe for the presence of a file by hash, couldn't an attacker learn something about the user's browsing history by checking whether, say, a game engine Wasm module is cached?

COS addresses this through two complementary mechanisms:

Crucially, this means an error is not a definitive answer. It might mean "not stored", or it might mean "stored, but the browser isn't telling you". Apps should always handle it the same way: fall back to the network.

Going back to the toy examples from before: the ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm runtime weighs in at 4,733 kB and is shared by every Transformers.js-powered app regardless of which AI model it uses. With COS, the first app to load it downloads it once and stores it under its SHA-256 hash with origins: '*'. Every subsequent app, whether on https://googlechrome.github.io, on https://rawcdn.rawgit.net, or any other origin, finds it in COS immediately. The 177 MB of duplicate Whisper model weights? Same story: Xenova/whisper-tiny.en gets downloaded once, recognized by hash the second time around, and served from COS in milliseconds. And of course, the same also happens for Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english.

Transformers.js itself is already piloting the COS API at the library level. Pull request #1549 introduced an experimental COS cache backend behind an opt-in flag. Enabling it takes a single line before you set up your pipeline:

Note the experimental_ prefix on the flag. It's intentional and signals that the underlying browser API has not yet been standardized and may change without a major version bump. With that flag set, Transformers.js resolves the SHA-256 hash for each Xet-tracked model file (the large ONNX weight files) by fetching the raw Xet pointer (example raw pointer file) and extracting its oid sha256: field. It then uses that hash as the key for navigator.crossOriginStorage. If the model is already in COS (because another site stored it there first), it's served instantly without a network round-trip. If not, it falls back to a regular download and stores the result in COS for the next caller. With the toy example, the advantage in practice is that Xenova/whisper-tiny.en and Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english (and of course ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm) only ever need to cross the ether once, regardless of how many different origins ask for them.

The toy example works just fine with Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, but of course you possibly wouldn't say no if the user already has any of the other Whisper variants in their COS cache. For example, the user might already have Xenova/whisper-large-v3, which, as the name suggests, is a lot larger than the tiny variant. Transformers.js's Model Registry makes being flexible about your models possible. If you know your app's needs can be addressed by, for example, any of Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, whisper-medium.en, or Xenova/whisper-large-v3, you can check the registry for the associated files for each model, probe for their existence in the COS cache (which may partially or completely contain the model resources you need), and then take a decision what model to choose eventually. The ModelRegistry.is_pipeline_cached() API directly integrates with COS (and of course the Cache API), so this operation is really ergonomic.

The COS API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, but you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow. Check out the source code of the extension and follow the usage instructions to get started.

With the extension installed, try the full end-to-end experience right now: open the first toy example with COS enabled, let it load Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, then open the toy example with COS enabled from the second origin. Instead of the 177 MB re-download you saw before, the model is served from COS in milliseconds. When you open the extension's popup window, you can see COS in action. If you View by Resource, you can see the resource with the SHA-256 hash 950978b1dbcbf250335358c1236053ba19a7f7849b33dc777f4421b72b7626fa shared across https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. It may not be obvious, but as you can verify by comparing the SHA-256 hash on Hugging Face, you're looking at https://huggingface.co/Xenova/whisper-tiny.en/blob/main/onnx/decoder_model_merged.onnx. For now, the extension is mostly aimed at power users like you. Once implemented in the browser, there will be a friendlier integration in the browser's Settings page. The screenshot below shows the extension's popup window with the View by Resource tab active, where you can see the shared resource with its hash and the two origins that have it in their COS cache.

If you're building your own Transformers.js app, the call to action is simple: add env.experimental_useCrossOriginStorage = true before your first pipeline() call, install the extension, and watch the duplicate downloads disappear from your Network tab. Every site that opts in makes the experience faster and cheaper for every other site's users. Opting in is completely risk-free: if the COS API isn't supported because the user doesn't have the COS extension installed, the code just falls back to the default path (the Cache API).

Transformers.js is not alone in experimenting with COS. WebLLM (opt-in, see documentation) and wllama (automatic, see PR) are likewise excited about this proposed API.

On the Chrome team, we're considering implementing the COS API natively in the browser. As an early stage proposal, we welcome feedback on the API, and the shape of the proposal itself. The Cross-Origin Storage repository is the place to file issues, express support, or open PRs.
