#9994. Entering the Geminispace

November 25, 2026 · About 13 minutes · Tags: blogsystem5, gemini

This article was originally published on Substack in the Blog System/5 newsletter and is replicated here for archival purposes.

On May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread. I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that.

However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/. The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post.

Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way.

A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and EndBASIC.

A terrible name, that is. Looking for information about Gemini these days is extremely hard, thanks to Google polluting the namespace with its own AI offering. Of course that’s not Project Gemini’s fault because Google’s thing came after them, but still, good luck finding stuff about this network.

Joking aside, let’s look at Project Gemini’s barebones front page:

… and break down the introductory and only paragraph:

Gemini is a new internet technology supporting an electronic library of interconnected text documents.

You can think of Gemini as a way to access a bunch of text-only pages, with links among them, so you can find information and follow links to additional resources. Instead of using http:// or https:// URL prefixes, you use gemini:// instead.

That’s not a new idea, but it’s not old fashioned either.

Exactly. Gemini is like the WWW, or “the web” in more colloquial/modern parlance. In fact, Gemini is a parallel community to the web. Obviously, that’s not a new idea because the web dates back to 1989, and we are now 37 years after that.

The idea is not unique either because Gopher, a much lesser-known option, exists as well. Surprisingly to me, I realized that Gopher came after the web in 1991 while researching this article. I had always assumed Gopher was first and that the web came to replace it because of Gopher’s rigidness. But that’s not quite what happened.

It’s timeless, and deserves tools which treat it as a first class concept, not a vestigial corner case.

Humans have shared written documents since around 3400–3100 BCE (roughly 5,100–5,400 years ago) in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, and that’s probably (hopefully?) not going away. It’s true, though, that at this point, text sharing is not the primary thing that the web does, as you well know. We have morphed the web from a document distribution tool into an app platform, for better or worse.

A little confession: I worked at Google for 12 years, starting right at the time they published Google Wave (2009), which to me marked the start of truly interactive web apps—more so than Gmail (2004) did. In the back of my mind, I knew I was helping turn the web into how we run apps, destroying the traditional desktop paradigm—a feeling I never liked. And… it happened. Obviously, it’d have happened without me, a little pawn in the game, but it bothered me regardless.

Gemini isn’t about innovation or disruption, it’s about providing some respite for those who feel the internet has been disrupted enough already.

(That comma splice hurts.) As we have established earlier, Gemini’s ideas are not new, so it’s indeed not innovative. And seeing how little people read these days, or even how unable to pay attention to long-form text they are, it’s not going to disrupt anything either. But respite is key: having a separate place where you know you’ll only find some sort of counter-culture sounds entertaining.

Fun fact: I wasn’t quite sure what respite meant and originally took it to be similar to spite. That meaning would have worked equally well here, if not better?

Here is the interesting thing. Gemini claims that it has been designed to minimize the chances of becoming bloated, and I’m not exactly sure how you can prevent that. For example: articles can provide links to images, but images are not auto-loaded. OK, says who? The auto-loading part is something the client browser controls, and it’d be trivial to create a Gemini browser, or modify an existing one, to auto-load and render images. That’d go against the spirit of Gemini, but if enough people wanted it, it’d happen. Same story as the browser wars.

And that’s the key: “enough people”. As long as Gemini stays under the radar and only like-minded people gravitate towards it, these properties will be maintained. But if for any reason it becomes more mainstream… unwanted changes will happen.

Gemtext is the native format of documents stored in the Gemini network, with a MIME type of text/gemini and a .gmi extension. Gemtext documents are typically grouped in capsules—which is just another name for “website”.

The format itself is like a super-diluted version of Markdown, supporting just these features:

Workable for sure, but weak. In my opinion, Gemini missed the boat of creating a truly semantical web, but for that you need additional primitives to represent more concepts. In any case, you can read through the long FAQ to know that this was discussed and eventually ruled against, so know that a lot of thought was put into its design.

Yet another fun fact: just two days ago, I stumbled upon “Good morning and welcome to my idea of a new web”: the proposal of a “browser” that just renders Markdown documents. This feels quite similar to the idea behind Gemini, but using a better (not a great) format with more markup abilities. And I say fun fact because, as I was learning about Gemini, I was imagining developing this exact alternate idea.

One curious bit is that Gemtext is also the format for subscription feeds. Sure, you can offer an RSS feed for your capsule, but RSS is a monster spec that feels out of place in a minimalistic network like Gemini’s. So you can abuse Gemtext to create a feed by creating a page that’s primarily links with a de-facto YYYY-MM-DD Title format. Again, it’s simple, and it works.

The big benefit of Gemtext’s simplicity is that clients can also be super-simple. You can rest assured that all clients will be able to display the same content, consistently. So far I’ve tried Elpher within Emacs, Lagrange on the desktop, and Buran on my Android phone. All are simple. All display text in the same way.

I definitely do not recommend using the Gemtext format to persist your original content, but that doesn’t mean you have to write in Gemtext. Which brings us to Markdown again.

All of the content you are reading in this blog is authored and stored as Markdown documents. Like many other people who still maintain a blog in this day and age, I started with a hosted platform (Blogger) and then experimented with Medium. But as soon as Medium became riddled with noise, I ran away. Unfortunately, escaping was difficult: the format that Medium spit out was frigging awful—almost as if it were designed to provide the illusion that you could export content, even if the content was nearly useless after the fact.

It was at that point that I committed to converting my golden copies to Markdown even though authoring in Markdown was more inconvenient. And believe me: it is inconvenient, especially when having to insert images. But now I own my content in a format that’ll survive for years to come.

Which brings us back to Gemtext. The thought that crossed my mind when I stumbled upon Project Gemini again three weeks ago and that triggered this whole thing was: can I write a script to convert my Markdown docs into a capsule? And with “I” I really mean AI, because this is the kind of experiment I was not going to code myself.

And of course I could. After just one simple prompt, I had a converted site that I could browse. Granted: the conversion Python script was literally awful, and the converted format was not great either, but having something I could play with inspired me to try harder.

So I threw everything away and started over, again with AI, to write a conversion tool for my blog (codenamed gengems for now) that takes the existing Hugo layout and spits out a capsule end-to-end in just 300 milliseconds while processing 1000 documents. The tool is obviously written in Rust, and by now supports enough configurable features that I’m increasingly tempted to throw Hugo away for the web version and create my own static site generator too. Because, you know, while Hugo works, it isn’t the greatest in usability and its recurrent incompatible changes are annoying. I’ll resist the urge to do that for now… I think.

Let’s dive a tiny bit into gengems. First of all, this second iteration is still entirely vibecoded. Oops, first sin. I have not looked at the code because it’s working for what I need it to do, it’s fast, and it’s not going to be used by anyone else… unless you want it, but then I’d probably rewrite it once more now that I know what the final feature set looks like.

Now, for this second iteration, I was so close to running out of my $20 weekly OpenAI quota that I pivoted from my favorite GPT 6.1 Sol model to GPT 6 Luna to see how far I could go. Luna is so cheap that you can do a ton with it, and I actually got gengems to work well enough within just a few iterations.

But oh dear. Luna is cheap, but it’s also kind of crap for coding. It stops half-way. It doesn’t think through enough corner cases. It doesn’t produce enough tests. The plans it produces are very vague. You have to be extremely prescriptive when asking it to do things and even that leads to mixed results. Out of curiosity, when my weekly cap was reset, I asked Sol to review what Luna did, and oh boy did it have things to say. From design problems to important missing tests, passing through outright bugs. I let it fix those issues, and I continued building with Sol.

Right now, I’m actually pretty happy with the results of gengems. I can configure the mapping of pages to templates in a much more explicit way than in Hugo. I can use MiniJinja for templating. I can specify cross-site links. I can handle inline links, figures, and even tables. I can generate archives/feeds for the site, for each year, for each month. I can process blog posts, and also standalone pages. All in all, the results are very satisfactory given the close-to-zero effort I put into it.

With the site exported to Gemtext, I needed a server. There are a lot of options out there, but the one that piqued my interest was Agate: a minimalistic Gemini server written, of course, in Rust. You run the binary pointing it at the directory containing the generated site and, voila, it works. Agate even takes care of auto-generating SSL certificates because all Gemini traffic is TLS-protected, and the fact that it’s automated is a relief because dealing with certificates is a pain.

But running Agate once, interactively, and making it serve in the background are different stories. I am running FreeBSD on my server and I could have used the prebuilt agate package, but then I encountered a crashing bug and wanted to add a feature, so I had to pivot to building from source. And, as you can imagine, Cargo leaves a lot to be desired if you want to install the resulting product to a running system.

Now, of course you can copy the built binary to, say, /usr/local/bin/agate, but there is typically much more than a binary in a distribution: think about documents, examples and, for a server program in particular, startup scripts. Mind you, Agate’s source tree does include a FreeBSD rc.d script, but it was buggy, insufficient, and it also required manual copying. So I created a PR to revamp the installation system based on earlier experience with setting up similar infrastructure in other Rust services I run.

I mentioned briefly above that I wanted to add a feature to Agate and that it was the reason I had to build from source. And that feature is… analytics, which are the second sin right there.

But wait a second. What are analytics? You do realize that Agate prints and saves a log of incoming connections (with IPs redacted by default), right? That’s par for the course for any Internet server out there, because in order to serve requests… well, the server actually needs to know what those requests are and where to send the responses to. So you can always analyze the log to gain some insights on traffic.

And that’s pretty much what I did. I just wired this exact same information to my own analytics service for visualization. The only thing I see are the pages that are being downloaded, when they are downloaded, and the originating country (computed from the requester’s IP after truncating the last octet to mask it). Essentially… good old page counters from the 1990s.

The way I implemented this is generic though: I extended Agate to add optional support for an SSI-style URL inclusion primitive and then added such a call to the capsule-wide footer template given to my Gemtext generator. As a high-level primitive, it can serve other purposes, like sourcing comments for each page by making the footer download a pre-rendered .gmi chunk. I haven’t implemented that yet in my comments service, but it should be pretty easy.

Sounds interesting? I might try to contribute this SSI feature upstream to Agate, but I predict that this collides with the goal of a lightweight server and that it’ll be rejected. But I’ll try anyway. I want to get the FreeBSD-related bug fixes and related improvements merged first, because those are helpful to everyone, I hope.

That’s about it! If you are in the U.S. you are about to have 4 days off, so spend that time falling into the Gemini rathole. And if you are elsewhere, do the same! It’s entertaining.

From now on, remember that you can also read this blog via gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/ if you want a super-fast, distraction-free experience. To get started, visit the Gemini software page for a long list of clients to choose from and install.

(Content also available at: gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/post/2026/11/entering-the-geminispace.gmi)

#9992. Hackers help themselves to 1Password's source code and customer data

An intruder planted malicious code in backend services, but the biz insists passwords are safe

1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code.

The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information.

1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata.

The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said.

Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected.

1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions.

The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as users must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address.

The company says it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens.

Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult.

1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork.

The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords.

The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK users. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords.

Customers aren't being asked to change their account passwords or Secret Keys, neither of which 1Password stores, although the company is warning users to be on the lookout for phishing attempts.

A list of email addresses belonging to people known to use a particular password manager is a handy thing for a phisher to have, especially when said password manager has just given them a plausible pretext for getting in touch. ®

#9991. Ambiguous Errors Are the Mind Killer

In which I express frustration at the widespread FUD caused by ambiguous errors in the software we write and consume.

I must not fear. Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little-death that brings total obliteration. I will face my fear. I will permit it to pass over me and through me. And when it has gone past I will turn the inner eye to see its path. Where the fear has gone there will be nothing. Only I will remain.

Have you ever written or encountered something you think would be an “ambiguous error”? No? How about HTTP 500 Internal Server Error? -EINVAL? Status.INTERNAL? Or even a {"status": "error"}?

Ambiguous errors, that is errors that are represented opaquely, are quite literally everywhere. Compared to happy-path return values, errors have long been second-class citizens across all software. I always felt that this was some abstractly “bad” thing, but it wasn’t until recently that I was able to put substance behind these feelings.

Software has boundaries, whether that be between my application and the libraries it consumes, the operating system it runs atop, or the remote services it calls out to. Boundaries are powerful! They let us hide immense complexity behind simple contracts — AWS S3 being the canonical example. But across a boundary, the only information I have to act on is exactly what you return to me.

So I’m left with two bad options. I can reverse-engineer your errors, in the process becoming a hated Hyrum’s Law perpetuator. Or I can throw up my hands and treat every catch or ? as if I were passing around a bomb. We consume tons of high quality, rigorously tested software, but can’t take advantage of it, because we don’t understand how it fails.

Worse, ambiguous errors are viral. Once you’ve consumed one, re-establishing what actually went wrong is far more work than just passing it forward. So you don’t try, and now your callers have the same problem.

Even Rust, with great support for strongly typed errors, isn’t immune. io::Error wraps the OS’s errno, itself a “god error” kept in line by the Linux kernel’s (very good!) docs. A NotFound from fs::remove_file is something most callers would consider a success, yet most code just ?s it upwards alongside everything else.

The usual Rust advice is anyhow for applications and thiserror for libraries, but every application can become somebody else’s library! Typed errors should become part of your API. Adding new error variants should be considered breaking changes. How your software fails is part of its contract.

Software can fail in countless ways, but a caller can only do a handful of things about it: retry, fix its input, give up, or blame someone else. Errors should encode enough meaning to fill in those gaps.

More concretely, at Modal we encounter an amusing variation of this. Running rollouts for Reinforcement Learning involves constructing sandboxed working environments, and when one fails, the trainer should be aware of how. Infrastructure failures should be thrown away, lest they bias training. But a reward-hacking model may simply learn to crash its sandbox if it thinks things are going sideways, in an attempt to escape penalization. Adding an error contract to this model allows the trainer to understand and account for these errors.

Writing the contract forces you to answer questions like “How exactly does my software fail?” and “How might someone want to react to those failures?“. You may find that your application can’t fail in a way your interface hinted was possible, or that you yourself can be more resilient to upstream failures. With agentic coding assistants, it’s more and more possible to actually do this exercise. List out every error from the leaves of your execution graph upwards, eliminate the ones that don’t make sense, and add stronger types to the rest.

#9990. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

#9989. UK government working 'around the clock' on Capita contingency plans

Minister says outsourcer should be 'absolutely ashamed' of pensions failures after CEO exits and shares plunge

The UK government is working "around the clock" on contingency plans for Capita contracts after the outsourcer's CEO quit and its shares plunged, a Cabinet Office minister told MPs.

Capita announced plans this week to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 after warning of sharply lower profits and further costs linked to its Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) contract.

The outsourcer "should be absolutely ashamed of its performance" on the £239 million contract, Sally Jameson, parliamentary secretary in the Cabinet Office, told MPs on Tuesday.

"We have seen evidence that it has stepped up in recent months and begun to rectify the problem, but it is inexcusable that it let the situation get to this point," she said.

Adolfo Hernandez stepped down as CEO with immediate effect on Monday, with finance chief Pablo Andres taking over. Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement.

In the House of Commons, Jameson was asked about the government's plans if Capita were unable to carry out the remainder of its contract given the outsourcer's performance on the CSPS.

"On contingency planning, it is important that we stabilize the situation and that Capita can continue to deliver the pension scheme. However, the government is working across departments, as we do in relation to all strategic suppliers, to ensure that the relevant contingency plans are in place. People are working around the clock on that," she said.

Jameson said contingency planning for the pension scheme was already underway before Monday's announcement, describing it as standard practice for major government suppliers.

She told the Chamber that the Cabinet Office was "currently arranging to meet the new CEO in the coming days" following Hernandez's departure.

The Register first exposed problems with Capita's CSPS portal last December. The site, serving 1.5 million current and former public servants, rejected login details even for newly created accounts, contained broken and circular links, and displayed dummy text.

In January this year, the Cabinet Office was forced to promise "interim support measures" for the CSPS following Capita's botched takeover, including 150 additional government staff to clear the backlog in cases.

Speaking in Parliament, Conservative MP Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the Public Accounts Committee, said there had been "some tragic and dreadful cases" since Capita took over administration last December.

"I heard of one poor lady who was living on benefits because she could not get the bereavement payments she needed after her sister's death. I have heard of a member of parliamentary staff, not far from this Chamber, who is having to delay his retirement by a year because he cannot even get a statement from the scheme."

The government has withheld nearly £10 million in contractual payments over Capita's performance. It is currently locked in negotiations over further penalties following the appointment of an auditor, first revealed in July. At the time, Hernandez apologized for Capita's performance but refused to commit to further compensation.

The National Audit Office and Public Accounts Committee have both launched probes into Capita's handling of the CSPS and its appointment as a contractor.

In February, The Register revealed a legal challenge to the government's award of the separate Synergy shared services contract to Capita. The deal covers HR and finance services across four Whitehall departments and associated arm's-length bodies. Rival bidder Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL, alleges Capita's bid was abnormally low and its proposed staffing raised concerns about delivery. Capita and the Department for Work and Pensions, which led the procurement, deny the allegations and say the competition was fair and open. Capita values the contract at £370 million.

The Public and Commercial Services Union is now calling on the government to scrap Capita's shared services contract with the DWP, citing the outsourcer's troubled handling of CSPS. ®

#9987. Granite 4.2 LLMs: How They're Built

A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.

TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B. These models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15T tokens with a five-phase strategy that extends the context window to 512K tokens, supervised fine-tuned on chain-of-thought, reasoning, and agentic-trajectory data, then post-trained with a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. That pipeline includes agentic RL, where the 8B and 30B models learn to act with tools inside real sandboxed environments. Every model has a thinking / non-thinking switch, a low-effort thinking mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions, and native tool calling. All Granite 4.2 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family. Earlier Granite releases were strong instruction-following assistants; Granite 4.2 adds explicit reasoning. Every model can produce a chain of thought before its answer and can run in thinking or non-thinking mode depending on how much deliberation a task needs. A low-effort mode falls between the two, spending a short reasoning budget on easy questions.

The three sizes (3B, 8B, and 30B) share the same architectural design and follow the same training pipeline (base model, SFT, then multi-stage RL), each at its own scale. All three are strong reasoners and instruction followers. The clearest capability split shows up in post-training. The 8B and 30B models additionally go through an agentic RL block that teaches them to operate as agents: calling tools, editing and running code, driving a terminal, and searching the web inside real environments. Every model supports native tool calling. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example, with vLLM), it emits tool calls in the OpenAI function-calling format and plugs into agentic harnesses without extra glue. Granite 4.2 is also supported in SGLang, see the SGLang cookbook for a ready-to-serve recipe.

The rest of this post walks through the build: architecture, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, the multi-stage RL pipeline, and results.

Granite 4.2 models are built on a decoder-only dense transformer architecture with the following core components:

Granite 4.2 models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five-phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre-training, phases 3–4 perform mid-training with progressively higher-quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long-context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase uses a distinct data mixture and learning-rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web-scale data toward more curated, high-quality sources.

The pre-training recipe closely follows the previous generation; for a detailed treatment of the data blend, phase schedule, and long-context extension, see the Granite 4.1 blog.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the base model into a reliable instruction-following, reasoning, and tool-using assistant. The SFT data mixture combines agentic (31.6%) and non-agentic (68.4%) data, totaling approximately 7.2 million samples, or roughly 100B tokens, of which about 65B are trainable.

The agentic corpus covers a broad range of domains, including software engineering (SWE, 69%), tool calling (12.1%), terminal use (8.0%), math (3.5%), search (0.8%), and action (0.2%). These samples and trajectories are generated using a diverse set of agent scaffolds and harnesses, including OpenHands, OpenCode, Terminus-2, SWE-agent, OpenResearcher, MiniSWE, OpenSeeker, EnvScaler, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex, and Goose. The agentic data combines samples from both open-source datasets and our own synthetically generated RL environments, spanning a variety of agent–harness combinations.

The non-agentic corpus consists of several major categories: instruction following (18.8%), coding (18.8%), math (14.6%), multilingual (7.0%), science (5.4%), reasoning (3.0%), and safety (0.8%).

We apply multiple stages of quality control before a sample enters the final SFT mixture. First, data from different sources is normalized and reformatted into a consistent OpenAI Chat format, making the conversation structure and tool interactions uniform across datasets and scaffolds.

We then use GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as LLM-based judges to assess sample quality. Low-scoring samples are removed, as are samples containing hallucinated or fabricated information, invalid tool interactions, or tool calls to functions that are not defined in the corresponding tool list. Several targeted, dataset-specific heuristic rules are also applied where appropriate to further improve quality and remove known sources of noise.

Finally, we perform both local and global deduplication. Deduplication is based on SHA-256 hashes computed over the combination of the tools and messages fields, removing duplicate samples both within individual data sources and across the overall SFT mixture.

The complete corpus is first globally shuffled to reduce ordering effects and ensure that samples from different domains are well mixed during training. The shuffled corpus is then partitioned into equally sized .parquet shards, which are tokenized using the model's tokenizer and chat template and prepared for large-scale distributed training.

Before launching the final large-scale runs, we tune hyperparameters on representative configurations, sweeping learning-rate schedules, initial learning rates, and warm-up ratios to find settings that train stably across model sizes. The final training configuration is summarized below:

For the 30B model, we additionally perform a second phase of SFT focused specifically on agentic coding. In this phase, agentic, SWE, and coding data are upsampled to increase their effective contribution to the training distribution, while approximately 16% of the mixture is retained as replay data from the original SFT corpus.

The 30B model is then fine-tuned for roughly one additional epoch at a lower learning rate of 3.0e-6. This targeted second phase increases the model's exposure to agentic coding trajectories without discarding the capabilities acquired during the initial SFT phase.

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage, multi-environment reinforcement learning pipeline. Rather than a single RL pass, we run a chain of focused stages spanning many environments: math, code, science, instruction following, tool use, and structured output, then software engineering, terminal use, and web search. Each stage is an independent RL run that targets one capability and warm-starts from the previous stage's checkpoint.

Figure 1. The staged RL curriculum. Foundational RL (verifiable rewards + skill boosters) runs for all sizes; the agentic RL block (SWE → Terminal → Search) runs for 8B and 30B only. Every model finishes with RLHF. Each stage is a separate GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint.

Every stage trains with asynchronous GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), so the generator and trainer halves of the loop never block on each other. A pool of generation workers keeps sampling responses and dropping the finished trajectories into a shared buffer; once the buffer holds a full step's worth, the trainer pulls that batch, takes an optimizer step, and streams the updated parameters back to the generator workers without pausing them. A refresh can land partway through a rollout, leaving a single trajectory stitched together from two adjacent policy versions. We allow this instead of paying to prevent it: the workers reuse their existing KV cache rather than rebuilding it after each refresh, and the one guardrail is a limit that keeps them from drifting more than a single update behind the trainer, which bounds how off-policy any sample can get. Whatever mismatch survives that limit is handled in the objective by truncated importance sampling, which clamps the train-versus-generation log-probability ratio to a fixed ceiling so a handful of stale tokens cannot dominate an update.

Advantages are group-relative with a leave-one-out baseline: each response is judged against the mean reward of the other samples drawn for the same prompt, which removes the need for a separate value network. To make this concrete, take RLVR, the first and longest-running stage: each step pairs 256 prompts with 16 sampled responses apiece for a 4,096-example batch, which the trainer consumes in a single optimizer step before the next rollout begins. Later stages keep this machinery unchanged and adjust only the per-stage shape, shown next.

The pipeline keeps a common backbone of hyperparameters across every stage, which makes the curriculum easier to run and compare. A handful of knobs are fixed everywhere:

What changes from stage to stage is the shape of each run: how many prompts and generations per step, how long the context is, whether the agent loop runs, and how hard we pull back toward the reference policy. The table below gives the exact settings for the 30B chain, stage by stage:

Parameters shown for the 30B model. Global batch size = prompts/step × generations/prompt (e.g. 256 × 16 = 4096 for RLVR). The 3B and 8B models use the same recipe and hyperparameters with fewer stages (see How the Three Sizes Differ); the stage list is what changes, not the knobs.

The KL schedule follows the reward type: explore freely where the reward is objective and verifiable (RLVR and SWE 2 run at KL 0), and stay close to the reference where the objective is preference, safety, or a narrow skill graft (RLHF and the code booster use KL 0.05). The rollout-turns column counts the environment interactions GRPO itself sees per rollout. In every case the model is trained on complete, real-environment trajectories.

Each stage is a separate RL run with a single objective and its own reward signal. When it finishes, its policy is exported to Hugging Face format and becomes the base model for the next stage, so the pipeline is a sequence of warm-starts:

The 8B and 30B models follow the full ladder. The 3B model takes a shortened path: foundational RL and alignment, without the agentic block.

A stage is defined mostly by how it is rewarded. Across the pipeline there are three reward types, and a single stage can use more than one:

Verifiable rewards are objective and hard to game, so the pipeline front-loads them. Judge- and preference-based rewards handle open-ended qualities that no checker can express. Agentic-outcome rewards are the sparsest: often a single bit at the end of a long tool-use trajectory.

RLVR is the foundational stage and the broadest data mix in the pipeline: a single blended dataset spanning many verifiable domains.

Each task type carries its own verifier, so the reward is grounded per example. RLVR runs for two rounds on 3B and 8B, and three on 30B. Each round is a fresh warm-started run on a re-weighted mix of public and internally curated RL data.

After RLVR, a few short booster stages sharpen specific capabilities that benefit from concentrated training focusing on the following domains:

Boosters are small, focused runs. A light KL penalty keeps the model close to its current behavior while nudging one skill.

In the agentic stages the model learns to act: call tools, observe results, and iterate inside a real environment, rewarded on whether the task was actually solved. These stages share the same shape: multi-turn tool use, real (not simulated) environments, sparse outcome rewards, and GRPO, warm-started from the coding-boosted checkpoint. They run in order: SWE → Terminal → Search.

Figure 2. The three agentic-RL environments. Each pairs a real harness with a real environment and a sparse, outcome-based reward. The 3B model runs none of these.

The final stage of every model is RLHF for human preference and safety. It optimizes against a generative reward model (GenRM) for preference, plus a safety reward covering jailbreak resistance and appropriate refusals. This stage uses the highest KL penalty in the pipeline, aligning tone and safety without eroding the capabilities the earlier stages built. In addition to human preference and safety alignment, this stage also applies a reasoning-length penalty to discourage overly verbose reasoning behavior acquired during earlier stages.

Same method and infrastructure; the difference is how far up the ladder each model goes.

3B is a strong foundational-RL model; 8B and 30B add the agentic-RL block on top, learning to act with tools in real environments.

Reinforcement learning at this scale needs infrastructure that can drive a training loop and a fleet of live environments at the same time. This matters most in the agentic stages, where every training example is a multi-turn rollout that edits code, runs commands, or browses the web. Granite 4.2's RL runs on two open components: NeMo-RL on the training side and NeMo-Gym on the rollout side.

Figure 3. The RL system. NeMo-RL drives the GRPO loop (Megatron-Core training backend, vLLM generation, and Megatron-Bridge for HF⇄Megatron weight conversion). NeMo-Gym orchestrates rollouts and hosts the tools, sandboxes, and reward/verifier calls as pluggable Resources.

That uniformity is what makes the staged curriculum above practical: a booster's rule-based checker and a full SWE sandbox present the same interface to GRPO.

This split is also what makes the asynchronous training loop described above physically possible: generation and policy updates live on separate GPU pools, so the expensive generation fleet — including the live agentic environments — stays busy instead of idling through optimizer steps.

Granite 4.2 was evaluated across agentic coding, general agentic and tool use, reasoning, chat and instruction following, and long context. The full benchmark table is below, followed by charts that break out the headline results by model size.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

The charts below break these results out by capability area.

Figure 4. Reasoning (pass@1). Scores rise consistently with model size across math (AIME25, HMMT), science (GPQA), and code reasoning (LiveCodeBench, SciCode).

Figure 5. Agentic coding resolve rates. The agentic-RL block is trained only for 8B and 30B; the 30B model leads across SWE-Bench variants and Terminal-Bench.

Figure 6. General agentic and tool-use benchmarks, reported for all three sizes.

We also released four quantized variants of the Granite 4.2 models for inference with vLLM. The models are converted to FP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using LLM Compressor, and to the GGUF format using the llama.cpp framework for reduced-memory deployment.

The FP8 version is quantized with dynamic per-channel weights and per-token activations. No calibration is used.

The NVFP4 and MXFP4 versions are quantized using GPTQ calibrated on 2K samples drawn from the SFT dataset. Max context length is 2K during calibration.

Conversion of the Granite 4.2 models to GGUF is done with the canonical llama.cpp tool as described in https://github.com/IBM/gguf#gguf-conversion--quantization.

We trained the Granite 4.2 language models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave, featuring:

This infrastructure delivers the high-bandwidth, low-latency communication required for efficient large-scale distributed training.

The training software stack is packaged into .sqsh container images, each giving a run a reproducible, portable environment with its SBSA-compatible CUDA targets, Linux aarch64 Python wheels, and GPU-specific binaries pinned. The large-scale SFT runs build on an NGC PyTorch base image (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12); the RL stack runs in its own NeMo-RL container.

Granite models support tool calling with integrated reasoning: the model reasons about which tool to call and why before calling it. Tools are defined with the OpenAI function definition schema.

Granite models can serve as the backbone for agentic coding tools. Because they support reasoning and tool calling through the OpenAI-compatible API, they integrate with popular agentic harnesses without extra adapters. Start the vLLM server, then follow the harness-specific instructions below.

OpenCode is an AI coding agent that runs in your terminal.

Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:

For full documentation, see opencode.ai/docs.

Pi is a minimal agent harness for AI-powered coding that runs in your terminal. It supports custom providers via a models.json configuration file.

Then select the granite-4.2-30b model with /model or Ctrl+L in the interactive session.

OpenHands is an AI software engineer that can plan, write code, and execute commands.

Install and launch OpenHands following the official installation guide.

Configure the LLM in the OpenHands settings with:

Note: The openai/ prefix is required when connecting to OpenAI-compatible endpoints like vLLM. Refer to the OpenHands local LLM documentation for detailed setup instructions, troubleshooting, and alternative installation methods.

#9985. How WinHelp files work

I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.

Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco. Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.

A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00, followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it. Most of them have names starting with a pipe: |SYSTEM holds the title and settings, |TOPIC holds the text, |FONT holds the fonts, |CONTEXT holds the topic names, and pictures live in files like |bm0.

The directory is a B+ tree, and so is every other index in the file, all with the same page layout.

All the text lives in |TOPIC, which is cut into fixed-size blocks. Each block can be LZ77 compressed, and positions in the file count bytes of the decompressed text, not of the file itself. Every block also takes up the same amount of that address space whether it fills it or not. In a typical file, each block gets 16 KB of space and only decompresses to about 4 KB, so reading has to skip the gap to the next block.

Inside the blocks, the text is a linked list of records. Some records start a new topic, and the rest hold its paragraphs, each with a formatting part and a text part. The text part can be compressed a second time, which is where it gets fun.

WinHelp's LZ77 is about as simple as compression gets. The data comes in groups: one flag byte, then up to eight items. Each bit of the flag byte, lowest first, says whether its item is a literal byte or a back-reference. A back-reference is two bytes, with 12 bits of distance and 4 bits of length:

The length is stored minus 3, since anything shorter isn't worth a back-reference. A distance of 0 means "repeat the byte I just wrote", and since the copy can read bytes it's still writing, x followed by a back-reference of length 5 becomes xxxxxx.

One fun quirk: some real files have back-references that reach behind the start of the data, where there's nothing to copy yet. helpdeco keeps its 4 KB window in a buffer that starts out full of zeroes, so those references just copy zeroes, and the files come out right that way. libhlp starts its window out zeroed too, instead of treating it as an error or reading off the front of the buffer.

On top of LZ77, a help file can swap its most common phrases for short codes, and there are two versions of this.

WinHelp 3.1 keeps the table in |Phrases. In the text, any byte from 1 to 15 starts a two-byte code, and every other byte is just itself:

The lowest bit of the code says whether a space follows the phrase. Phrases usually end at a word, so that saves a byte most of the time.

The Windows 95 help compiler added a fancier scheme, called Hall compression, with the phrases split across |PhrIndex and |PhrImage. Here, the lowest bits of each byte say what kind of byte it is. If the lowest bit is clear, the rest of the byte picks one of the first 128 phrases, so the most common ones fit in a single byte. Ending in 01 starts a two-byte code for the rest of the table, 011 starts a run of literal bytes, 0111 means a run of spaces, and 1111 means a run of zero bytes. For the runs, the upper bits hold the length minus one, since a run of nothing would be a wasted byte.

|PhrIndex doesn't store where each phrase starts. It stores how long each one is, packed into as few bits as it can get away with. Each length is a unary count in steps of some power of two, followed by the remaining low bits to add on top. The step size is set once for the whole file.

My first version always read at least one remainder bit. That works until a file uses a step of one, where there's no remainder to store. Then every length reads one bit too many, and everything after the first phrase is garbage. The fix was a single bits > 0 check.

When a help author wrote a topic, they gave it a context string, a name like SaveFile. You'd expect a link to store the position of the topic it points to, but it actually stores a hash of the target's name. To follow a link, you hash its target name the way WinHelp does and look the result up in |CONTEXT, which maps hashes to positions.

Each byte goes through a lookup table that gives uppercase and lowercase letters the same values, so links are case insensitive. The table's entries are signed, so anything at or above 0x80 subtracts instead of adding. Get that wrong and almost every hash still comes out right, so it's really easy to miss. Oh, and an empty name hashes to 1, not 0, because that's what WinHelp does.

Text doesn't store its own formatting. A paragraph says "switch to font 4", and |FONT says font 4 is the bold one. Links are drawn the same way. WinHelp underlines a link by switching to an underlined font, so libhlp has to tell that underline apart from underlining the author actually asked for.

WinHelp is older than Unicode, so text is stored in whatever Windows code page the author used, which might be a double-byte one for East Asian languages. Sometimes the file's language ID says which one. When it doesn't and the text is mostly non-ASCII, libhlp guesses the code page from the text itself.

Then there's WinHelp 3.0, the version from Windows 3.0, which is different enough to almost be its own format. Its topic blocks are 2 KB and never compressed, its records give the distance to the next record instead of its position, its topic headers are 12 bytes instead of 28, and its links point at topic numbers instead of hashes. libhlp reads it, but it took its own commit.

And then there are the files that only share the extension. Borland's help compiler and MS-DOS QuickHelp both made .hlp files that have nothing else in common with WinHelp, so libhlp just turns those away.

It reads the text, titles, tables, emphasis, links and pictures of every WinHelp version I know of, from 3.0 to the Windows 95 compiler, and it bounds checks everything. Paperback uses it to open .hlp files, so if you've got an old one sitting around, now you can read it.

#9984. Microsoft hotpatches hotpatch that could crash Windows Server 2025

Expiring IPv6 routes can bring affected systems down, though corrective update doesn't require a restart

Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security update that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires.

The patch for the patch, KB5138318, addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes. When a route timer expires, affected servers can halt with error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE).

Issued on November 25, the corrective update takes effect without requiring a restart, according to Microsoft.

KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE means the kernel has detected corruption of a critical data structure and stopped the system. Microsoft has identified route-timer expiry as the trigger but hasn't explained the underlying coding fault.

Good to see the operating system being protected against the impact of the corruption. Less good for administrators wondering why their servers have suddenly misbehaved.

Lansweeper puts Windows Server 2025 at 7 percent of the servers it monitors, compared with 32 percent for Server 2022 and 33 percent for Server 2019. Only systems with the affected hotpatch and networking configuration are implicated.

Microsoft's Windows Server updates have not gone well over the last few months, with out-of-band updates issued in September, October, and November. An out-of-band update to deal with a problem introduced in a hotpatch (in this case, KB5131077) therefore carries with it a certain sense of inevitability.

Hotpatches are a way of getting OS security updates on a Windows Server without requiring a restart and so are, in theory, a boon for administrators keen on maximizing uptime. According to Microsoft, in addition to faster installations and better protection, there is "lower workload impact with less need to restart your machine."

Avoiding a planned restart is less of a selling point when the alternative is an unplanned crash. ®
